# Medical billing staff for US practices, without the hiring headache

Claims pile up when one person is out. Denials sit unworked. Prior authorizations eat your front desk's afternoon. This site explains how practices and billing companies solve those problems, including when a dedicated remote billing team makes sense and when it doesn't. When you want help, we route your request to a [vetted, approved vendor](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/).

**Get a free staffing assessment.** Tell us a little about your practice and we'll connect you with a vetted billing staffing vendor. It takes about a minute.

## Who this site helps

- **Solo and small practices** where the office manager is also the biller, the scheduler and the person who calls payers.
- **Specialty groups** such as behavioral health, physical therapy, chiropractic, labs and ambulatory surgery centers (ASCs), where payer rules and authorizations are specialty-specific.
- **Multi-location groups** that need consistent billing processes across sites.
- **Practice and billing managers** who need more hands on the A/R, denial or authorization queues without adding local headcount.
- **Medical billing companies** that need to add trained staff as they win new clients.

## Common billing problems we write about

- **Denials that never get reworked.** In a vendor survey of billing professionals, 40% reported an increase in denials over the prior year ([Tebra, 2025](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)). Federal transparency data show HealthCare.gov insurers denied 20% of in-network claims in 2023 ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/private-insurance/claims-denials-and-appeals-in-aca-marketplace-plans-in-2023/)).
- **Aging A/R.** Claims nobody has followed up on after 30, 60 or 90 days.
- **Prior authorization workload.** Physicians surveyed by the AMA reported an average of 39 prior authorization requests per physician per week, taking about 13 hours of physician and staff time ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/fixing-prior-auth-nearly-40-prior-authorizations-week-way)).
- **Eligibility surprises.** Coverage changes discovered after the visit, not before.
- **Hiring and turnover.** In the same vendor survey, 38% of billers said they struggle to find qualified candidates ([Tebra, 2025](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)).

Read more: [Revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) · [Denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/) · [How to reduce AR days](https://medicalbillingteam.com/reduce-ar-days/)

## The remote billing team model, explained

A remote billing team is not a software product and not a full billing takeover. It is dedicated people working your queues:

- **They work in your systems.** Your practice management system, clearinghouse and payer portals, with access you grant and can revoke.
- **They follow your rules.** Your fee schedules, your write-off policy, your escalation path.
- **They are dedicated.** The same people every day, so they learn your payers and your providers.
- **You keep control.** You own the process and the payer relationships. The staffing provider recruits, employs, trains and supports the staff.

Typical roles include billing specialists, A/R follow-up specialists, eligibility and benefits verification (VOB) staff, prior authorization coordinators, payment posters, denial follow-up specialists and admissions or intake support.

We think a staffing model fits some practices well and others not at all. Our [cost guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/) compares in-house, outsourced and remote options side by side, and [medical billing outsourcing: three models](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-outsourcing/) explains the trade-offs.

## HIPAA comes first

If anyone outside your practice will touch patient data, HIPAA is the first question, not the last. Before remote or offshore billing staff log in to anything, you should expect:

- **A business associate agreement (BAA)** with the agency, because a company that handles billing involving protected health information on your behalf is a business associate under HIPAA ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)).
- **Minimum necessary, role-based access.** Staff see only what their job requires.
- **Strong access controls:** unique logins, multi-factor authentication, secure remote access (VPN or virtual desktop) and no local downloads or printing.
- **Documented training, risk analysis and a breach-reporting process.**

One more thing to know: **there is no official "HIPAA certification"** for companies or staff. HHS's Office for Civil Rights states that it does not endorse, certify or recommend specific technology or products ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html)). Be cautious of anyone who claims to be "HIPAA certified."

[Read the full HIPAA guide for outsourced and offshore billing staff →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/)

## Technology in medical billing

AI and automation now touch most of the revenue cycle: claim scrubbing, denial prediction, eligibility checks and electronic prior authorization, which CMS-0057-F requires impacted payers to support through APIs by January 1, 2027 ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/cms-interoperability-and-prior-authorization-final-rule-cms-0057-f)). People still own the queues and review the output. Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [See technology in medical billing and the latest updates →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

## Short FAQ

### What is a remote medical billing team?

It is one or more dedicated billing and revenue cycle staff who work remotely inside your systems, under your workflows, doing tasks such as eligibility checks, prior authorizations, claim follow-up, payment posting and denial work. You direct the work; a staffing provider handles recruiting, employment and supervision.

### Should I outsource medical billing or keep it in-house?

It depends on volume, specialty and how much control you want. In-house staff give the most control but are the hardest to hire and cover. A full-service billing company takes over the function. Dedicated remote staff sit in between: you keep the process, and a provider handles hiring.

### What are the main medical billing staffing models?

Three: an in-house team you employ, a full-service billing company that runs billing for you, and dedicated remote staff who work your queues in your systems while a staffing provider employs them. Many practices mix models, such as in-house billing plus remote verification or A/R help.

### How much does medical billing staffing cost?

In-house cost is wages plus benefits and overhead; BLS reports a May 2025 median hourly wage of $23.32 for billing and posting clerks. Billing companies often charge a percentage of collections, while staffing providers usually charge per staff member. Our cost guide compares them.

### Do remote or offshore billers need a business associate agreement?

Yes. A company whose staff handle protected health information for your billing is a business associate under HIPAA and needs a signed BAA before access. No company or person can be officially 'HIPAA certified,' so be wary of that claim.

### How do you choose approved vendors?

We publish our criteria, including signing a BAA before any PHI access, dedicated staff working in your systems, US billing experience, references on request and no 'HIPAA certified' claims. This site is operated by Alliance Global Solutions, currently our only approved vendor.

### How do I get started, and do you need patient information?

Use the short form on this page or the longer contact form. Practice-level details such as specialty and number of providers are enough. Never send patient information. Your request may be referred to Alliance Global Solutions, our affiliated approved vendor.

See the [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/), [cost guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/) and [how we vet vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-we-vet-vendors/) for detail.

# What is revenue cycle management (RCM) in healthcare?

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** Revenue cycle management (RCM) is the set of administrative and clinical-support steps a healthcare provider uses to get paid for its services, from scheduling and insurance verification through coding, claims, payment posting, denial management and patient collections. Good RCM means clean claims go out quickly, payments are posted accurately, denials are worked and prevented, and nothing ages past filing or appeal limits.

Every patient visit starts a financial process that can take weeks or months to finish. Revenue cycle management is the name for managing that process end to end. This guide explains each step, the metrics used to measure RCM, common problems, how to improve it, and how practices staff it. For the staffing side in depth, see our companion pillar on [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/).

## The revenue cycle, step by step

### 1. Scheduling and patient registration
The cycle begins when a patient books. Front-desk staff, or a [virtual medical receptionist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/virtual-medical-receptionist/), capture demographics and insurance details. Errors here flow through to every later step.

### 2. Insurance eligibility and benefits verification
Staff confirm active coverage, plan type, cost sharing and coordination of benefits before the visit. See our guide to [insurance verification services](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/). For treatment centers, this is the [verification of benefits (VOB)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/treatment-center-vob/) by level of care.

### 3. Prior authorization and referrals
Services that require payer approval need it before they're performed. Physicians in an AMA survey reported 39 prior authorizations per physician per week ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/fixing-prior-auth-nearly-40-prior-authorizations-week-way)). See [prior authorization specialists and outsourcing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/).

### 4. Provider credentialing and enrollment
Providers must be enrolled with each payer, with confirmed effective dates, or their claims deny. See [medical credentialing services](https://medicalbillingteam.com/credentialing-services/).

### 5. Documentation and coding
Clinical documentation is translated into diagnosis (ICD-10-CM) and procedure (CPT/HCPCS) codes. ICD-10 updates take effect October 1 each year ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/icd-10-codes)). See [outsourcing medical coding](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hire-remote-medical-coders/).

### 6. Charge entry
Coded services are entered into the practice management system with the right fees, modifiers and provider information.

### 7. Claim submission and scrubbing
Claims are checked for errors and submitted to payers, usually through a clearinghouse. Rejections (claims not accepted for processing) are corrected and resubmitted quickly.

### 8. Payment posting
Payments from electronic remittance advice (ERAs) and EOBs are posted, reconciled to deposits, and checked against contracted rates. Remittances explain adjustments using claim adjustment reason codes (CARCs) from X12 ([X12](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes)). See our [denial code guides](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/#denial-code-guides).

### 9. Denial management
Denied claims are categorized, corrected, resubmitted or appealed, and root causes are fed back upstream. KFF found HealthCare.gov insurers denied 20% of in-network claims in 2023 ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/private-insurance/claims-denials-and-appeals-in-aca-marketplace-plans-in-2023/)). See [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/).

### 10. Accounts receivable follow-up
Unpaid and underpaid claims are worked by age and dollar value until resolved. Medicare's claim filing limit is one calendar year from the date of service ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/regulations-and-guidance/guidance/manuals/downloads/clm104c01.pdf)). See [what an AR specialist does](https://medicalbillingteam.com/ar-specialist/) and [days in AR](https://medicalbillingteam.com/reduce-ar-days/).

### 11. Patient billing and collections
Patient balances (deductibles, coinsurance, self-pay) are billed, explained and collected, with payment plans where appropriate.

### 12. Reporting and improvement
Leaders review KPIs monthly and fix the causes of problems, not just the symptoms.

## Front end, middle and back end

People often group the steps into three parts:

| Part | Steps | What goes wrong |
|---|---|---|
| Front end | Scheduling, registration, eligibility, prior authorization, credentialing | Wrong insurance, missing authorizations, unenrolled providers |
| Middle | Documentation, coding, charge entry | Coding errors, missing modifiers, charge lag |
| Back end | Claims, posting, denials, A/R, patient collections | Unworked denials, aging A/R, underpayments |

Most back-end problems start at the front end, which is why denial work should always feed causes back upstream.

## Key RCM metrics

- **Days in A/R:** how long, on average, it takes to collect.
- **Clean claim rate:** claims accepted on first submission.
- **Denial rate:** denied claims as a share of claims submitted.
- **Net collection rate:** payments as a share of what you're contractually owed.
- **First-pass resolution:** claims paid or resolved on first submission.
- **A/R over 90 days:** the share of receivables at risk.

Benchmarks vary by specialty, payer mix and method, so track your own trend month over month. Definitions and formulas are in our [RCM staffing guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) and the [billing audit checklist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/checklist/).

## Why revenue cycle management matters

Payers set filing and appeal deadlines, administrative work keeps growing, and denials go unpaid if nobody works them. KFF found consumers appealed fewer than 1% of denied in-network claims in HealthCare.gov plans in 2023 ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/private-insurance/claims-denials-and-appeals-in-aca-marketplace-plans-in-2023/)). That's patient-side data, but the lesson carries over: denials that no one works don't get paid. Good RCM turns more of the care you provide into collected revenue, with less rework.

## How to improve revenue cycle management

1. **Verify eligibility and benefits before every visit,** not just for new patients.
2. **Track authorizations** with expirations and visit limits.
3. **Keep credentialing current** and tell billing about effective dates.
4. **Cut charge lag:** enter charges within a day or two of service.
5. **Scrub claims and work rejections daily.**
6. **Post payments daily** and flag zero-pay and underpaid lines.
7. **Own the denial queue,** sorted by payer and reason, worked weekly at minimum.
8. **Work A/R by dollar value and age,** with a documented next step on every claim.
9. **Review KPIs monthly** and fix one root cause at a time.
10. **Make sure each queue has enough people.** Many of these steps fail simply because no one has the time.

Use our free [medical billing audit checklist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/checklist/) to find where to start.

## Who does RCM? In-house, outsourced or dedicated staff

- **In-house team:** full control; you carry hiring, training, turnover and coverage. BLS reports a median wage of $23.32 an hour for billing and posting clerks (May 2025) ([BLS](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ocwage.t01.htm)), before benefits.
- **RCM company (outsourced RCM services):** runs most or all of the cycle, often for a percentage of collections. See [medical billing outsourcing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-outsourcing/).
- **Dedicated remote staff:** people who work only on your account, in your systems, under your direction. See [offshore medical billing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/offshore-medical-billers/) and [hiring a medical billing virtual assistant](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hire-remote-medical-billers/).

Compare total cost with our [staffing cost guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/).

## RCM and HIPAA

Everyone in the revenue cycle handles protected health information. Any outside company whose staff access PHI on your behalf is generally a business associate and needs a business associate agreement before access ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). There is no official "HIPAA certification." See our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/).

## Technology

Technology touches every RCM stage: automated eligibility at intake, AI coding assistance, claim scrubbing, denial prediction and electronic prior authorization under CMS-0057-F, with payer API deadlines of January 1, 2027 ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/cms-interoperability-and-prior-authorization-final-rule-cms-0057-f)). Vendors are also building payer-policy intelligence into the front end to prevent denials before care is delivered ([Fierce Healthcare](https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/health-tech/thoreau-backed-ensemble-penelope-health-partner-tackle-payer-denials-upstream)). Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. ## FAQ

### What is revenue cycle management in healthcare?

The set of steps a provider uses to get paid for care, from scheduling and insurance verification through coding, claims, payment posting, denial management, A/R follow-up and patient collections.

### What are the main steps of the revenue cycle?

Scheduling and registration, eligibility verification, prior authorization, credentialing, documentation and coding, charge entry, claim submission, payment posting, denial management, A/R follow-up, patient collections and reporting.

### When does the revenue cycle begin?

When the patient schedules. Registration and insurance details captured then affect every later step.

### How can a practice improve revenue cycle management?

Verify eligibility before every visit, track authorizations, keep credentialing current, reduce charge lag, work rejections and denials on a schedule, post payments daily, follow up on A/R by value and age, and review KPIs monthly.

### What is the difference between RCM and medical billing?

Medical billing usually means creating, submitting and following up on claims. RCM is broader and includes front-end steps like eligibility, authorization and credentialing, plus reporting and process improvement.

# Revenue cycle management staffing: roles, workflow, KPIs and costs

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** Revenue cycle management (RCM) staffing means putting people on each step that turns a patient visit into payment: eligibility, coding, charge entry, claims, denials, A/R follow-up and payment posting. Practices staff it in-house, through a billing company, or with dedicated remote staff working in the practice's own systems. The right mix depends on volume, specialty and how much control you want to keep.

Revenue cycle management (RCM) is every step between a patient booking an appointment and your practice collecting the last dollar for that visit. When one step is understaffed, the effect shows up later, as denials, aging A/R and write-offs. This guide covers the RCM workflow, the roles behind it, the KPIs worth tracking and the three main ways practices and billing companies staff it: in-house, outsourced and dedicated remote or offshore teams.

## What RCM staffing means

RCM staffing is the work of putting trained people on each part of the revenue cycle. For a solo practice, that might be one person juggling everything. For a multi-location group or a billing company, it is a team with defined queues: eligibility, authorizations, coding, charge entry, claims, denials, A/R and posting.

There are three common models:

1. **In-house staff.** You recruit, employ, train and manage billing staff locally.
2. **Outsourced RCM.** A billing or RCM company takes over the function, typically under a contract priced as a percentage of collections or per claim. You trade control for convenience.
3. **Dedicated remote or offshore RCM staff.** A staffing provider recruits and employs staff, often in another country, who work full time in *your* systems and follow *your* processes. You keep control of the workflow and payer relationships.

Many organizations mix models, for example keeping a local billing manager and coder while adding remote staff for eligibility, posting and A/R follow-up.

## The RCM workflow, step by step

### 1. Eligibility and benefits verification

Before the visit, staff confirm active coverage, plan type, copays, deductibles, coordination of benefits and whether a referral or authorization is required. Errors here cause problems later: in a 2025 vendor survey of billing professionals, coordination of benefits issues were the most commonly cited denial reason (45% of respondents), followed by non-coverage (39%) ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)). Read more in our [eligibility verification and prior authorization guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/).

### 2. Prior authorization

Staff submit and track authorization requests, attach clinical documentation and follow up on pending decisions. The AMA's survey of 1,000 physicians found practices complete an average of 39 prior authorization requests per physician per week, and that 40% of physicians have staff who work exclusively on prior authorizations ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/fixing-prior-auth-nearly-40-prior-authorizations-week-way)). Under the CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule, impacted payers (Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service and managed care; FFE qualified health plans are excluded from this particular timeframe requirement) must send decisions within 72 hours for expedited requests and seven calendar days for standard requests, starting in 2026, and must give a specific reason for denials ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/cms-interoperability-and-prior-authorization-final-rule-cms-0057-f)).

### 3. Medical coding

Certified coders assign CPT, HCPCS and ICD-10-CM codes from provider documentation. Code sets change on a schedule: ICD-10-CM updates generally take effect October 1 each year ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/icd-10-codes)), and the AMA's CPT Editorial Panel maintains CPT ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/cpt/cpt-overview-and-code-approval)). Coding is skilled work; remote coders should hold recognized credentials and specialty experience.

### 4. Charge entry

Charges, modifiers, units, place of service and rendering provider are entered into the practice management system, often with a charge review step to catch missing documentation or mismatched codes before claims go out.

### 5. Claims submission and scrubbing

Claims are scrubbed for errors, submitted through a clearinghouse, and rejections (claims the payer or clearinghouse never accepted) are corrected quickly. Timely filing limits matter: Medicare generally requires claims within one calendar year of the date of service ([CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 1, §70](https://www.cms.gov/regulations-and-guidance/guidance/manuals/downloads/clm104c01.pdf)), and commercial payer limits are often shorter.

### 6. Denial management

Denied claims are categorized by reason, corrected, resubmitted or appealed, and the root cause is fed back to the front end. HealthCare.gov insurers denied 20% of in-network claims in 2023 according to KFF's analysis of federal data, and consumers appealed fewer than 1% of denied claims ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/private-insurance/claims-denials-and-appeals-in-aca-marketplace-plans-in-2023/)). That data covers one market segment, but it shows why someone needs to own the denial queue. See [denial management basics](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/).

### 7. A/R follow-up

A/R specialists work unpaid claims by age and dollar value, check status on payer portals, call payers and escalate. The goal is to resolve claims before they age past timely filing or appeal limits. See [how to reduce AR days](https://medicalbillingteam.com/reduce-ar-days/).

### 8. Payment posting

Payments from ERAs (835 files), paper EOBs, lockbox deposits and patient payments are posted and reconciled to the bank. Accurate posting is how you spot underpayments, incorrect adjustments and denials that arrive inside a "paid" remittance.

### Supporting functions

- **Credentialing and payer enrollment**, so providers can bill payers at all.
- **Patient statements and patient A/R.**
- **Reporting**, so the practice sees the KPIs below every month.

## RCM roles you can staff

| Role | What they do | Remote-friendly? |
|---|---|---|
| Eligibility / VOB specialist | Verifies coverage and benefits before visits | Yes |
| Prior authorization coordinator | Submits and tracks authorizations | Yes |
| Medical coder | Assigns CPT/HCPCS/ICD-10 codes | Yes, with credentials |
| Charge entry specialist | Enters and reviews charges | Yes |
| Billing / claims specialist | Scrubs and submits claims, works rejections | Yes |
| Denial management specialist | Works denials and appeals | Yes |
| A/R follow-up specialist | Works unpaid claims, calls payers | Yes |
| Payment poster | Posts and reconciles payments | Yes |
| Credentialing specialist | Manages enrollment and re-credentialing | Yes |
| Billing manager | Owns process, reporting and escalation | Often local |

## RCM KPIs, defined

Definitions vary slightly between organizations. Pick one definition, document it, and use it consistently.

- **Days in A/R:** total accounts receivable divided by average daily charges (for example, total charges over the last 90 days divided by 90). It estimates how long, on average, it takes to collect.
- **Clean claim rate:** the share of claims accepted and processed on first submission without edits, rejections or requests for more information.
- **Denial rate:** denied claims (or denied dollars) divided by total claims (or dollars) submitted in a period. Track by payer and reason code.
- **Net collection rate:** payments collected divided by the amount you were contractually entitled to collect (charges minus contractual adjustments) for the period. It shows how much collectible revenue you actually captured.
- **First-pass resolution rate:** the share of claims paid in full, or otherwise fully resolved, after the first submission with no further touches.
- **A/R over 90 (or 120) days:** the share of A/R older than 90 or 120 days.

**About benchmarks:** published benchmarks vary widely by specialty, payer mix and methodology, and many come from member-only surveys or vendor marketing. We don't publish a benchmark number unless we can cite a public source. Instead, trend your own numbers monthly and compare with specialty data you trust. The [Medical Billing Health Checklist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/checklist/) includes a simple KPI worksheet.

## In-house vs outsourced vs dedicated remote RCM: how to compare costs

We won't give you invented price ranges. Here is how to build a fair comparison with your own numbers.

**In-house cost** is more than salary. Add wages, payroll taxes, benefits, paid leave, recruiting, training, software seats, equipment, workspace and management time. Public data help as a starting point: the BLS reports a May 2025 median hourly wage of $23.32 for billing and posting clerks ([BLS OEWS](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ocwage.t01.htm)) and a median annual wage of $51,140 for medical records specialists, the BLS category that includes medical coders ([BLS OOH](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/medical-records-and-health-information-technicians.htm)). Benefits add materially on top: in private industry, benefits averaged 30.0% of employer compensation costs in June 2026 ([BLS ECEC](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ecec.nr0.htm)). Then add the cost of vacancies, because unworked queues keep aging while you hire.

**Outsourced RCM cost** is usually a percentage of collections, a per-claim fee, or a hybrid. Ask what is included (coding? credentialing? patient statements? appeals?), how "collections" is defined, minimums, setup fees and exit terms. Model the fee against your actual monthly collections.

**Dedicated remote or offshore staff** are usually priced per full-time staff member per month or per hour. Compare that rate against fully loaded in-house cost for the same role, then add your own costs: management time, onboarding, software seats and secure remote access (for example, a VDI setup).

**Non-cost factors** matter as much as price: control of the workflow, visibility into queues, turnover risk, coverage during absences, HIPAA safeguards, and how quickly you can add or remove capacity. Our [medical billing staffing cost guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/) walks through a worksheet.

## Choosing an RCM staffing partner

Whatever model you pick, ask:

- Which roles can you staff, and what is the experience level for my specialty?
- Will staff be dedicated to us, and who supervises them day to day?
- How do you handle HIPAA: BAA, access controls, training, incident response? (See our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/).)
- How will we measure performance, and what reporting do we get?
- What happens if a staff member leaves?
- What are the contract length, notice period and exit terms?

Be wary of any vendor that guarantees a specific reduction in denials or A/R days before seeing your data. Results depend on your payers, specialty, documentation and starting point.

## Where a remote RCM team fits

A dedicated remote team tends to fit when you have steady, queue-based work (eligibility, posting, A/R, denials), systems that support secure remote access, and someone in-house who can own the process. It fits less well if your processes are undocumented or your billing system can't support remote access securely.

This site is operated by [Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/), which provides remote staff (US-based management and admin; staff in the Philippines, Colombia and other countries); you can read about its [remote medical billing and RCM staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/) on the company's own site. If you'd like a second opinion on your RCM staffing, request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/).

**Approved vendor:** [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), which operates this site, provides dedicated remote staff for this work and signs a business associate agreement with each client before any PHI access. See [approved vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/) and [how we vet vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-we-vet-vendors/).

## Technology

RCM teams increasingly pair people with automation: eligibility bots, claim scrubbers, denial-prediction tools and electronic prior authorization, which CMS-0057-F requires impacted payers to support through APIs by January 1, 2027 ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/cms-interoperability-and-prior-authorization-final-rule-cms-0057-f)). Staffing still matters, because someone has to own each queue and handle the exceptions automation can't. Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

## FAQ

### What is revenue cycle management staffing?

It means filling the roles that move a patient encounter from scheduling to final payment: eligibility and benefits verification, prior authorization, coding, charge entry, claim submission, denial management, A/R follow-up and payment posting. You can staff these roles in-house, outsource the whole function, or add dedicated remote or offshore staff who work in your systems.

### What is the difference between outsourced RCM and an offshore RCM team?

Outsourced RCM usually means a vendor runs the revenue cycle for you, often for a percentage of collections. An offshore RCM team is a staffing arrangement where dedicated staff abroad work your queues under your direction. Some vendors combine both.

### Which RCM KPIs should a small practice track first?

Start with days in A/R, denial rate, clean claim rate and net collection rate. They are straightforward to calculate from most practice management systems and show where the cycle is slowing.

### Is there a standard benchmark for days in A/R?

Benchmarks vary by specialty, payer mix and data source, and many industry benchmark reports are member-only. Track your own trend month to month and compare with specialty-specific data from sources you trust, rather than relying on a single generic number.

### Can remote RCM staff do medical coding?

Yes, if they hold the right credentials and specialty experience. Coding is a skilled role; ask for certification details and test candidates on your specialty's documentation before they code live claims.

# HIPAA and outsourced medical billing staff: what to check before anyone logs in

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

*General information, not legal advice. Talk to your own healthcare attorney or compliance adviser about your situation.*

**Short answer:** Before outsourced or offshore billing staff touch patient data, have a signed business associate agreement, limit access to the minimum necessary, and require strong technical controls: unique logins, MFA, secure remote access and no local downloads. Add documented training and a breach-notification process. There is no official "HIPAA certification," because HHS does not certify vendors, so ask for evidence of specific safeguards instead.

Billing work runs on patient data. Names, dates of birth, member IDs, diagnosis and procedure codes and payment details all sit on the screens your billing staff use every day. So when you bring in outsourced, remote or offshore billing staff through an agency, HIPAA is not a box to tick at the end. It shapes which agency you choose, how the contract is written, how access is set up and what happens if something goes wrong.

This guide explains the main HIPAA concepts that apply when a staffing agency provides dedicated billing staff, and ends with a checklist of questions to ask any agency, including ours.

## First, a myth: there is no "HIPAA certification"

You will see agencies and freelancers describe themselves as "HIPAA certified." There is no such official credential. The HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR), which enforces HIPAA, says plainly that it "does not endorse, certify, or recommend specific technology or products" ([HHS, Guidance on HIPAA & Cloud Computing](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html)). Training companies issue certificates of course completion, and independent auditors can assess security programs, but neither is a government HIPAA certification.

What matters is evidence of specific safeguards: a signed business associate agreement, documented policies, training records, a current risk analysis and technical controls you can verify. We don't claim to be "HIPAA certified," and you shouldn't accept that claim from anyone.

## Why an agency is usually a business associate

HIPAA's rules apply directly to **covered entities** (health plans, clearinghouses and health care providers that conduct standard electronic transactions such as claims) and to their **business associates**. HHS defines a business associate generally as a person or organization, other than a member of the covered entity's workforce, that performs functions or services on behalf of a covered entity involving the use or disclosure of protected health information (PHI). HHS lists **billing, claims processing and practice management** among the examples ([HHS, Business Associates](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)).

A staffing agency whose people work your claims, check eligibility or post payments in your systems is therefore typically a business associate. As a general rule of HIPAA law (not a description of any particular vendor's arrangements): a billing company that serves practices is often itself a business associate, so if it adds agency staff, the agency becomes a **subcontractor business associate**, and HHS says a business associate must have a BAA with its subcontractor before disclosing PHI to it ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)).

Business associates are not just contractually bound. Since the HITECH Act, they are directly liable for complying with the Security Rule's safeguards and certain Privacy Rule provisions ([HHS, Summary of the Security Rule](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/laws-regulations/index.html)).

## The business associate agreement (BAA)

HIPAA permits you to share PHI with a business associate only after you obtain "satisfactory assurances," in the form of a BAA, that it will safeguard the information ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). According to HHS, a BAA must, among other things:

- describe the permitted and required uses and disclosures of PHI;
- state that the business associate will not use or further disclose PHI except as the agreement permits or the law requires;
- require compliance with applicable Security Rule requirements;
- require reporting of security incidents and breaches of unsecured PHI;
- require that subcontractors agree to the same restrictions through their own BAAs; and
- address return or destruction of PHI at the end of the relationship, where feasible.

HHS publishes [sample business associate agreement provisions](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/covered-entities/sample-business-associate-agreement-provisions/index.html). Have your counsel review any BAA rather than relying on the agency's template alone.

**Practical tip:** sign the BAA before you create a single login. No PHI should move during interviews or trials without one.

## PHI handling and the "minimum necessary" standard

The Privacy Rule asks covered entities and business associates to make reasonable efforts to use, disclose and request only the **minimum necessary** PHI for the purpose, and to restrict workforce access based on role ([HHS, Summary of the Privacy Rule](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/laws-regulations/index.html)). For billing teams, minimum necessary in practice looks like:

- A payment poster gets posting screens and remittance files, not full clinical charts.
- An A/R follow-up specialist sees the claims and payer correspondence in their queue, not every patient in the system.
- An eligibility specialist uses payer portals and scheduling data, not visit notes.
- PHI is never pasted into personal email, chat apps, unapproved AI tools or spreadsheets on personal drives.

Behavioral health and substance use disorder programs carry extra rules. Records covered by 42 CFR Part 2 have their own consent and redisclosure limits; HHS notes that compliance with the 2024 Part 2 final rule was required by February 16, 2026 ([HHS, Part 2](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/hipaa-part-2/index.html)). See our [behavioral health billing guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/behavioral-health-billing/).

## Access controls to expect

The Security Rule is "technology neutral." It requires access control, audit controls, integrity controls, person or entity authentication and transmission security, but lets each organization choose reasonable and appropriate measures based on its risks ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/laws-regulations/index.html)). For remote and offshore billing staff, these are common, sensible controls to ask about:

- **Unique user IDs.** No shared logins, ever. Each person's activity should be traceable.
- **Multi-factor authentication (MFA)** on your practice management system, clearinghouse, payer portals, email and the agency's own systems.
- **Secure remote access.** A VPN, or better, a virtual desktop (VDI) so PHI stays on your servers or cloud and is only displayed remotely.
- **No local downloads, printing or USB storage.** Endpoint controls that block saving files, screenshots where feasible, and removable media.
- **Role-based access** mapped to each job, reviewed regularly, and removed the same day someone leaves.
- **Managed, encrypted company devices** with current patches and endpoint protection, rather than personal computers.
- **Activity logging and audit review.** Logs of who accessed what and when, reviewed on a schedule.
- **Physical controls.** For office-based teams, controlled facility access and clean-desk rules; for home-based staff, private workspaces and screen-privacy rules.

## Workforce training

The Security Rule requires security awareness training for all workforce members and appropriate sanctions for people who violate policies ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/laws-regulations/index.html)). Ask the agency for:

- HIPAA privacy and security training at onboarding and at least annually;
- phishing and social-engineering awareness;
- client-specific training on your policies, payer portals and escalation paths;
- signed confidentiality agreements; and
- training records you can review.

## Audits and risk assessments

Both covered entities and business associates must perform an accurate and thorough **risk analysis** of threats to electronic PHI, manage those risks, and periodically evaluate their safeguards ([HHS, Security Rule summary](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/laws-regulations/index.html)). When you add an agency:

- Update your own risk analysis to include the new remote access paths and locations.
- Ask when the agency last completed its risk analysis and what it changed as a result.
- Ask whether it has had an independent security assessment (for example, a third-party audit or penetration test) and whether it will share a summary.
- Agree in writing on your right to request documentation. HHS notes that HIPAA does not expressly require vendors to allow customer audits, but customers may require additional assurances through the BAA or service agreement ([HHS, Cloud Computing FAQ 10](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html)).

## Breach notification

Under the Breach Notification Rule, if a breach of unsecured PHI occurs at or by a business associate, the business associate must notify the covered entity **without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days** after discovery, and provide, to the extent possible, the identity of affected individuals ([HHS, Breach Notification Rule](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/breach-notification/index.html)). The covered entity then has its own obligations to notify individuals, HHS and, for larger breaches, the media.

Many practices negotiate a much shorter reporting window in the BAA. Ask the agency to walk you through its incident response plan: who detects an incident, who calls you, and how fast.

## Offshore considerations

HIPAA does not prohibit offshore work. In its cloud guidance, HHS says the HIPAA Rules "do not include requirements specific to protection of electronic protected health information (ePHI) processed or stored by a CSP or any other business associate outside of the United States," but warns that overseas outsourcing "may increase the risks and vulnerabilities to the information or present special considerations with respect to enforceability" ([HHS, Cloud Computing FAQ 9](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html)). Practical steps:

- **Keep PHI onshore where possible.** With VDI, data stays in your US-hosted systems and offshore staff only view it.
- **Know the legal entity.** Confirm which company signs the BAA, where it is incorporated, and whether a US entity is accountable.
- **Check payer and state rules.** Some payer contracts, Medicaid programs and government plans restrict offshore access to member data. Check before you assign offshore staff to those accounts.
- **Plan for continuity.** Ask about power, internet redundancy and backup work sites.
- **Document it in your risk analysis**, including country-specific risks.

## Questions to ask any billing staffing agency

Print this list and use it on every agency call, including with us.

1. Will you sign our BAA (or offer one our counsel can review) before any access to PHI?
2. Which legal entity signs, and do you use any subcontractors who would touch PHI? Do they sign BAAs too?
3. When did you last complete a HIPAA security risk analysis? What changed afterward?
4. Have you had an independent security assessment? Can you share a summary?
5. Do your staff use unique logins and MFA on every system?
6. Do staff work through VDI or VPN? Can they download, print, screenshot or use USB storage?
7. Are devices company-managed and encrypted? Who patches them?
8. How do you enforce minimum necessary and role-based access?
9. What background checks do you run on staff?
10. What HIPAA training do staff complete, how often, and can we see records?
11. Do staff work from an office, from home, or both? What physical safeguards apply?
12. What is your incident response plan, and how fast will you notify us of a suspected incident?
13. How do you remove access on the day someone leaves?
14. How do you handle Part 2 records, if we have them?
15. Do you claim to be "HIPAA certified"? (The right answer is that no such official certification exists.)

## How this site handles your information

Our forms never ask for patient information, and we ask you not to submit any. We collect only business contact and practice-level details. See our Privacy Policy.

## FAQ

### Is there such a thing as HIPAA certification?

No. There is no official HIPAA certification for companies or individuals. HHS's Office for Civil Rights says it does not endorse, certify or recommend specific technology or products. Private training courses may issue certificates, but these are not government certification of HIPAA compliance.

### Does a medical billing staffing agency need to sign a BAA?

If the agency or its staff will create, receive, maintain or transmit protected health information on your behalf, such as by working claims in your billing system, the agency is generally a business associate and HIPAA requires a business associate agreement before PHI is shared. Confirm your situation with your own counsel.

### Can offshore staff access PHI under HIPAA?

HIPAA does not ban offshore work. HHS guidance on cloud services says the rules do not include requirements specific to PHI handled outside the US, but notes that overseas arrangements may increase risk and raise enforceability concerns. Those risks should be addressed in your risk analysis and safeguards.

### How quickly must a business associate report a breach?

Under the Breach Notification Rule, a business associate must notify the covered entity without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovering a breach of unsecured PHI. Many BAAs set a shorter deadline.

### What does minimum necessary mean for billing staff?

It means making reasonable efforts to use, disclose and request only the minimum PHI needed for the task. For billing staff, that usually means role-based access limited to the queues, screens and payers they actually work.

# Medical billing staffing cost: in-house vs outsourced vs remote staff

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** An in-house biller costs their wage plus benefits and overhead. BLS puts the median wage for billing and posting clerks at $23.32 an hour (May 2025), and benefits average 30% of private-industry compensation costs (June 2026). Billing companies usually charge a percentage of collections, while remote staff are priced per full-time person. Compare all three with a fully loaded worksheet, not just the hourly rate.

"How much does it cost?" is the first question practices ask about billing help, and the honest answer is: it depends on your volume, specialty and what you're comparing. Instead of quoting price ranges we can't back up, this guide shows you how to compare three common models using your own numbers and public wage data.

The three models:

1. **In-house staff** you hire and employ.
2. **Outsourced billing company** that runs billing for you.
3. **Dedicated remote staff** from a staffing provider, working in your systems.

For the bigger picture of roles and workflow, see our [revenue cycle management staffing guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/).

## Model 1: In-house billing staff

### What you pay

Salary is the visible part. The full cost includes:

- **Wages.** The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a May 2025 national median hourly wage of $23.32 for billing and posting clerks, with a mean annual wage of $51,070 ([BLS OEWS](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ocwage.t01.htm)). For medical records specialists, the BLS category that includes medical coders, the May 2025 median was $51,140 per year ([BLS OOH](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/medical-records-and-health-information-technicians.htm)). Local wages vary widely, so check your metro area in BLS data.
- **Benefits and payroll taxes.** In private industry, benefits averaged 30.0% of total employer compensation costs in June 2026, and wages the other 70.0% ([BLS ECEC](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ecec.nr0.htm)).
- **Recruiting and onboarding.** Job ads, interview time, background checks, training time before the person is productive.
- **Software and equipment.** Practice management seats, clearinghouse fees attributable to the user, computer, phone, workspace.
- **Supervision.** The hours a manager spends reviewing work and answering questions.

### What it's good for

Direct control, on-site collaboration with providers and front desk, and deep familiarity with your practice over time.

### Watch-outs

Single points of failure (one biller on vacation means nothing gets worked), recruiting difficulty, and turnover. In a 2025 vendor survey, 38% of billing professionals said they struggle to find qualified candidates and 28% cited rising wages they can't afford ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)).

## Model 2: Outsourced billing company

### How pricing usually works

Billing companies commonly charge:

- a **percentage of collections** (the most common model for practices);
- a **per-claim** fee; or
- a **flat monthly** fee, sometimes with minimums.

We don't publish typical percentages because we haven't found a reliable public source for them, and quotes vary with specialty, volume and scope. Get at least two written quotes and compare them on the same basis.

### Questions that change the real price

- What does "collections" include? Patient payments? Capitation? Refunds netted out?
- What is included: coding, credentialing, patient statements, patient calls, appeals, old A/R cleanup, reporting?
- Are there setup fees, minimum monthly fees or fees for old A/R?
- What are the contract term, termination notice and data return terms?
- Who owns the payer relationships and portal logins?

### What it's good for

Practices that want to hand off the whole function and don't want to manage billing staff at all.

### Watch-outs

Less day-to-day visibility, less control over priorities, and cost that rises with your collections even if the workload doesn't.

## Model 3: Dedicated remote billing staff

### How pricing usually works

Staffing providers typically charge a monthly or hourly rate per full-time staff member. You direct the work in your systems; the provider recruits, employs and supports the staff.

### Your costs on top of the rate

- **Management time** to assign work, review output and answer questions, especially in the first month.
- **Onboarding** on your procedures and payers.
- **Software seats** for each user.
- **Secure remote access**, such as a virtual desktop (VDI) or VPN with multi-factor authentication. See our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/) for what to require.

### What it's good for

Practices and billing companies that want dedicated capacity and control without local hiring, especially for queue-based work: eligibility, prior authorization, payment posting, A/R follow-up and denials.

### Watch-outs

You still own the process. If your workflows aren't documented, remote staff will struggle, just as a new local hire would. Time-zone coverage, payer contract restrictions on offshore access and HIPAA safeguards all need to be settled up front.

## A side-by-side comparison

| Factor | In-house | Outsourced billing company | Dedicated remote staff |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pricing basis | Wages + benefits + overhead | % of collections, per claim or flat | Per staff member (monthly/hourly) |
| Control of workflow | Full | Limited | Full (you direct) |
| Who manages staff | You | Vendor | You direct; provider employs/supports |
| Systems | Yours | Often vendor's or yours | Yours |
| Coverage for absences | You arrange | Vendor | Provider can backfill (confirm in contract) |
| Scales with | Headcount | Collections | Headcount |
| HIPAA arrangement | Workforce member | Business associate (BAA) | Business associate (BAA) |

## Worksheet: compare with your own numbers

1. **Monthly workload.** Claims per month, eligibility checks per day, authorizations per week, open A/R by aging bucket.
2. **Staff needed.** Roughly how many full-time people that workload requires (ask your billing lead).
3. **In-house cost per FTE.** Local wage × hours + benefits (BLS: benefits ≈ 30% of private-industry compensation costs) + recruiting, software, equipment, supervision ÷ 12.
4. **Outsourced cost.** Quoted percentage × average monthly collections + any minimums or add-on fees.
5. **Remote staff cost.** Quoted monthly rate × FTEs + your software seats + remote access + management time.
6. **Risk adjustments.** Cost of a vacancy month (unworked claims aging), turnover frequency, and the value of control and visibility to you.

The [Medical Billing Health Checklist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/checklist/) includes this worksheet in printable form.

## Hidden costs people forget

- **Vacancies.** When a biller leaves, A/R keeps aging. Some claims can hit timely filing limits; Medicare generally allows one calendar year from the date of service ([CMS Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 1](https://www.cms.gov/regulations-and-guidance/guidance/manuals/downloads/clm104c01.pdf)) and many commercial payers allow less.
- **Owner time.** Physicians and managers who "just help with billing" are an expensive labor source.
- **Rework.** Denials that are corrected late cost more staff time than claims done right the first time. See [denial management basics](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/).
- **Switching costs.** Data migration, contract exit fees and retraining when you change models.

## Which model fits?

- **Choose in-house** if you have steady volume, can recruit locally and want everything on-site.
- **Choose an outsourced billing company** if you want to hand off the whole function and accept less control.
- **Choose dedicated remote staff** if you want control and dedicated capacity, have documented workflows, and can support secure remote access.

Many practices combine models: a local billing manager plus remote specialists for specific queues.

This site is operated by [Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/), which provides remote staff; you can read about its [dedicated medical billing staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/) on its own site. If you want help working through the worksheet, request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/). We'll tell you if another model makes more sense.

**Approved vendor:** [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), which operates this site, provides dedicated remote staff for this work and signs a business associate agreement with each client before any PHI access. See [approved vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/) and [how we vet vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-we-vet-vendors/).

## Technology

Automation changes the staffing math but doesn't remove it: tools can shrink manual eligibility and claim-status work, while people still work denials, appeals and exceptions. When you compare costs, include software and AI tool fees, and confirm that any tool vendor handling PHI signs a BAA ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. ## FAQ

### How much does outsourced medical billing cost?

Billing companies commonly price as a percentage of collections, a per-claim fee or a monthly fee. The right comparison is the fee applied to your actual collections and claim volume, compared with your fully loaded in-house cost. Ask exactly what services are included and how collections are defined.

### What is the fully loaded cost of an in-house medical biller?

Wages plus payroll taxes, benefits, paid leave, recruiting, training, software licenses, equipment, workspace and supervision time. BLS data show benefits averaged 30% of private-industry employer compensation costs in June 2026, so salary alone understates the cost.

### Are remote medical billing staff cheaper than in-house staff?

Often the hourly rate is lower, but you should compare total cost, including your management time, onboarding, software seats and secure remote access, against the fully loaded cost of a local hire for the same role.

### Is a percentage-of-collections fee better than paying for staff?

It depends on your volume and needs. Percentage pricing scales with collections and bundles management, but you give up some control. Staffing pricing is predictable and keeps control in-house, but you manage the process.

### What hidden costs should I include?

Vacancies and turnover, overtime, aging A/R while positions are unfilled, write-offs from missed timely filing limits, and the time owners or managers spend doing billing themselves.

# Technology in medical billing: AI, automation and what's changing

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** Technology is changing medical billing in five main places: AI that helps code, scrub claims and predict denials; automation for eligibility checks and claim status; electronic prior authorization, which CMS-0057-F requires impacted payers to support through APIs by January 1, 2027; payer-policy data used to prevent denials before care is delivered; and AI assistants that help staff draft appeals and work queues. People still have to own the work: someone has to check the output, handle exceptions and follow up with payers.

This hub explains, in plain language, where AI and automation fit in the revenue cycle, what rules are driving change, and what it means for staffing. The **Latest updates** section below is refreshed regularly from our weekly news scan. Every item is dated and linked to its source.

## Where technology fits in the revenue cycle

### AI coding assistance
Computer-assisted and AI coding tools suggest codes from clinical documentation. They can speed up coding, but coders still review suggestions against documentation and payer rules, especially for modifiers and bundling (see [CO-97](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-97/)). Code sets change on a schedule; ICD-10 updates take effect October 1 each year ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/icd-10-codes)). See [outsource medical coding](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hire-remote-medical-coders/).

### Claim scrubbing and denial prediction
Scrubbers check claims for missing or invalid data before submission, which targets errors like those behind [CO-16](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-16/). Newer tools use payer rules and past adjudication data to flag claims likely to deny. Large RCM vendors are building payer-policy intelligence into the front end so requirements are visible before care is delivered ([Fierce Healthcare, Oct 13, 2026](https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/health-tech/thoreau-backed-ensemble-penelope-health-partner-tackle-payer-denials-upstream)).

### Eligibility and benefits automation
Electronic eligibility checks return coverage and benefit details in seconds, and batch checks can run ahead of the schedule. They don't always show carve-outs, authorization rules or out-of-network details, which is why [insurance verification](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/) and [treatment center VOBs](https://medicalbillingteam.com/treatment-center-vob/) still often need a phone call.

### Electronic prior authorization and CMS-0057-F
The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F) requires impacted payers to make decisions within 72 hours for expedited and seven calendar days for standard requests, give specific denial reasons, and build prior authorization APIs by January 1, 2027 ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/cms-interoperability-and-prior-authorization-final-rule-cms-0057-f)). The AHA advises hospitals and health systems to prepare for significant changes to PA workflows and payer interactions as those provisions take effect ([AHA, Oct 15, 2026](https://www.aha.org/news/headline/2026-10-15-aha-launches-new-website-prior-authorization)). See [prior authorization specialists and outsourcing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/).

### Credentialing and enrollment tools
Credentialing platforms track documents, expirations and application status, and Medicare enrollment runs through CMS's online PECOS system ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/enrollment-renewal/providers-suppliers/chain-ownership-system-pecos)). See [credentialing services](https://medicalbillingteam.com/credentialing-services/).

### AI assistants for billing teams
General-purpose and RCM-specific AI assistants can help staff summarize payer policies, draft appeal letters, organize call notes and prioritize A/R work. Use them only in tools your organization has approved for PHI, under a BAA where the vendor handles PHI, and with a person reviewing anything that goes to a payer or patient.

### Payer-side AI and program integrity
Payers and regulators use AI too. CMS says it's piloting AI to flag suspicious Medicaid billing patterns before payment, and a CMS official acknowledged that "a lot of things" about its AI-supported prior authorization pilot (WISeR) "are not working" ([Nextgov/FCW, Oct 15, 2026](https://www.nextgov.com/artificial-intelligence/2026/10/cms-hopes-quadruple-provider-suspensions-over-next-six-months-official-says/416640/)). Accurate coding and documentation matter more as payer review becomes automated.

## What technology doesn't replace

- Someone who owns each queue and follows up until claims are resolved
- Judgment on exceptions, appeals, write-offs and patient conversations
- Payer phone calls when portals and APIs don't answer the question
- Human review of AI output before it reaches a payer or patient

## HIPAA and AI tools

Any vendor whose tool creates, receives, maintains or transmits PHI on your behalf is generally a business associate and needs a BAA ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). Check where data goes, whether it's used to train models, and who can access it. See our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/).

## Getting help

Alliance Global Solutions, which operates this site and is currently our only [approved vendor](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/), also helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. See its [featured vendor profile](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/). To talk through your setup, [request help](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/); your request may be referred to Alliance Global Solutions. Its [administrative virtual assistants](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/administrative/) page describes the support roles that often work alongside these tools.

## Latest updates

- **Oct 15, 2026: AHA prepares hospitals for the Jan. 1, 2027 prior authorization deadline.** The AHA launched a prior authorization resource site as major provisions of CMS-0057-F take effect Jan. 1, 2027. [Source: AHA](https://www.aha.org/news/headline/2026-10-15-aha-launches-new-website-prior-authorization)
- **Oct 15, 2026: CMS official says parts of the WISeR AI prior-auth pilot "are not working."** CMS is also piloting AI to flag suspicious Medicaid billing before payment. [Source: Nextgov/FCW](https://www.nextgov.com/artificial-intelligence/2026/10/cms-hopes-quadruple-provider-suspensions-over-next-six-months-official-says/416640/)
- **Oct 13, 2026: Ensemble and Penelope Health partner to bring payer-policy intelligence into RCM.** The aim is to move denial management upstream into denial prevention. [Source: Fierce Healthcare](https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/health-tech/thoreau-backed-ensemble-penelope-health-partner-tackle-payer-denials-upstream)

## FAQ

### How is AI used in medical billing?

Common uses include coding suggestions, claim scrubbing, denial prediction, eligibility automation, payer-policy lookups and AI assistants that help staff draft appeals and prioritize work. People still review the output and handle exceptions.

### What does CMS-0057-F require for prior authorization technology?

Impacted payers must build prior authorization APIs by January 1, 2027, and meet decision timeframes of 72 hours for expedited and seven calendar days for standard requests, with specific denial reasons.

### Will automation replace billing staff?

Automation reduces manual steps, but someone still owns each queue, follows up with payers, handles exceptions and reviews AI output before it reaches a payer or patient.

### Do AI tools need a BAA?

If the vendor's tool creates, receives, maintains or transmits PHI on your behalf, the vendor is generally a business associate and needs a BAA.

# Medical credentialing services: what's included and how to choose

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** Medical credentialing services handle the paperwork and follow-up that get providers approved by insurance payers and keep them enrolled. A service typically gathers documents, keeps provider profiles current, submits payer and Medicare (PECOS) applications, follows up until effective dates are confirmed, and tracks expirations and revalidation. It's usually priced per provider or per application, or covered by a dedicated staff member.

If you're adding providers, opening a location or joining new payer networks, credentialing is on the critical path to getting paid. This page explains what a credentialing service does, how to compare options, and what to ask before you hand over provider files. For the day-to-day role, see our guide to the [credentialing specialist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/credentialing-specialist/). It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

## What medical credentialing services include

Most provider credentialing services cover some or all of the following:

- **Document collection and verification:** licenses, DEA registration where applicable, board certification, malpractice coverage, education, work history and identifiers such as the NPI.
- **Profile maintenance:** keeping shared credentialing databases current and re-attesting on schedule.
- **Commercial payer enrollment:** applications, network participation requests and contract follow-up.
- **Medicare enrollment:** CMS runs Medicare enrollment through PECOS, its online enrollment system, and requires periodic revalidation ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/enrollment-renewal/providers-suppliers/chain-ownership-system-pecos)). CMS also warns that PECOS applications can be deleted automatically for inactivity, which is one reason consistent follow-up matters.
- **Medicaid enrollment** through each state's process.
- **Hospital and facility privileges** support, if needed.
- **Tracking:** expirations, re-credentialing cycles and revalidation dates, with reminders.
- **Status reporting:** a tracker showing every application, its status and the next step.

## Why practices outsource credentialing

Credentialing is detail-heavy, deadline-driven and lumpy. It spikes when you hire, then drops to maintenance. When it lands on an office manager with no time, applications stall, effective dates get missed and claims for a new provider deny. A service or dedicated specialist gives the work an owner.

Billing companies often add credentialing as a service line for their clients, which makes a dedicated remote credentialing specialist especially useful when you credential many providers across many payers.

## Service models and pricing

| Model | How it's usually priced | Good fit |
|---|---|---|
| Credentialing company | Per provider, per application or monthly maintenance fee | Occasional enrollment needs; you want it fully handled |
| Billing company add-on | Bundled or per provider | You already outsource billing |
| Dedicated remote specialist | Monthly or hourly per staff member | Steady volume; billing companies; multi-location groups |
| In-house | Salary plus benefits | Frequent hiring and a manager to own it |

We don't publish generic price ranges because they vary widely by scope. Ask every option to price the same list of providers, payers and tasks.

## What to ask a credentialing service

1. Which payers and states do you work with regularly?
2. Who keeps the provider profiles current, and how often do you re-attest?
3. How do you track applications, and can we see the tracker directly?
4. How do you handle Medicare (PECOS) and Medicaid enrollment and revalidation?
5. How do you notify billing of confirmed effective dates?
6. How do you secure provider data (SSNs, license details) and who can access it?
7. Will you sign a business associate agreement if your staff will also see patient information?

## Security and HIPAA

Credentialing files contain sensitive provider information such as Social Security numbers and license details, so access should be limited and secured. If credentialing staff will also touch patient data (for example, while helping with claims), a BAA is needed first ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). Alliance Global Solutions signs a business associate agreement (BAA) with each client before any of its staff access protected health information. There is no official "HIPAA certification"; ask about specific safeguards instead ([HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/)).

## Credentialing connects to the rest of the revenue cycle

Enrollment problems show up downstream as eligibility mismatches, [prior authorization](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/) problems and denials. A provider billed before their effective date, or not linked to the right group or location, creates denials that are hard to fix later. Make sure your credentialing owner tells billing the moment an effective date is confirmed.

You can read about its [administrative virtual assistants](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/administrative/) or its [medical billing staffing services](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/). To talk through your credentialing workload, [request help](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/); your request may be referred to Alliance Global Solutions. See [how we vet vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-we-vet-vendors/).

See [approved vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/) and [how we vet vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-we-vet-vendors/).

## Technology

Credentialing automation tracks documents, license and malpractice expirations, and application status across payers, and Medicare enrollment is handled online through PECOS ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/enrollment-renewal/providers-suppliers/chain-ownership-system-pecos)). Tools reduce missed renewals, but payer follow-up and corrections still need a person. Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. ## FAQ

### What do medical credentialing services include?

Typically document collection and verification, credentialing database maintenance, commercial payer enrollment, Medicare (PECOS) and Medicaid enrollment, revalidation and expiration tracking, and status reporting.

### How are credentialing services priced?

Commonly per provider, per application or as a monthly maintenance fee. A dedicated remote specialist is usually priced per staff member. Ask each option to price the same scope.

### What is PECOS?

PECOS is CMS's online system for Medicare provider and supplier enrollment. CMS requires periodic revalidation and notes that inactive PECOS applications can be deleted automatically.

### Is credentialing the same as payer enrollment?

No. Credentialing verifies a provider's qualifications; enrollment adds the provider to a payer's network or program with an effective date so claims can be paid.

### Does a credentialing service need a BAA?

If its staff will access patient information, yes. Credentialing files also contain sensitive provider data, so require secure, limited access either way.
