# Virtual medical assistants for billing and front-office work

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** A virtual medical assistant is a remote staff member who handles administrative work for a practice, such as eligibility checks, prior authorization follow-up, appointment reminders, data entry, payment posting and inbox management. A virtual assistant is not a clinical medical assistant and shouldn't do clinical tasks. Because the role touches patient data, require a BAA and secure access before day one.

"Virtual medical assistant" is a broad term. In practice it usually means remote administrative help for an overloaded front desk or billing team. This guide covers what a virtual assistant can and can't do, how the role fits with billing, and how to set it up safely. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

## What a virtual medical assistant can do

**Front-office and scheduling support**
- Appointment confirmations and reminder calls
- Insurance card and demographic updates in the practice management system
- Referral and records-request tracking
- Inbox, fax and portal message triage (non-clinical routing)

**Billing-adjacent work**
- Eligibility and benefits checks before visits (see [eligibility verification](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/))
- Prior authorization submissions and follow-up (see [prior authorization specialist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/))
- Charge entry from structured encounter forms
- Payment posting support and simple reconciliation
- Patient statement questions and payment plan setup, following your scripts

**Practice admin**
- Credentialing paperwork and expiration tracking (see [credentialing specialist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/credentialing-specialist/))
- Report preparation and data cleanup

## What to keep in-house or with licensed staff

- Clinical tasks, triage, medical advice or anything that requires a license
- In-person work: check-in, collecting payments, rooming patients
- Decisions on write-offs, refunds and policy exceptions (the assistant can prepare them, but a manager approves)

Medical assistants in a clinic are a different occupation with clinical duties; a virtual administrative assistant isn't a substitute for that role.

## Why practices use virtual assistants

Administrative load is a major pressure on small practices. Prior authorization alone accounted for about 13 hours a week of physician and staff time in an AMA survey ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/fixing-prior-auth-nearly-40-prior-authorizations-week-way)). Hiring is also hard: in a 2025 vendor survey, 38% of billing professionals said they struggle to find qualified candidates ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)). A virtual assistant can take repeatable administrative tasks off the front desk so in-office staff can focus on patients.

## Virtual assistant or dedicated biller?

| If your biggest problem is... | Consider |
|---|---|
| Phones, reminders, eligibility and paperwork | A virtual medical assistant |
| Unworked A/R and denials | A dedicated [AR specialist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/ar-specialist/) |
| Claims going out late or with errors | A dedicated remote biller |
| All of the above | A small team with defined queues |

## HIPAA and security setup

A virtual assistant who sees schedules, insurance information or billing records handles PHI. Before day one:

- sign a BAA with the staffing provider or contractor ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html));
- create unique logins with MFA, and use secure remote access through a virtual desktop or VPN;
- grant only the access the tasks require (minimum necessary);
- block local downloads, printing and personal devices; and
- train on HIPAA and your policies, and keep records.

There's no official "HIPAA certified" virtual assistant. See our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/) for the safeguards to ask about.

## How to start

1. **List the tasks** that eat the most front-desk and billing time each week.
2. **Write simple procedures** for the first two or three tasks, with scripts for patient calls.
3. **Start with a defined schedule** that overlaps your office hours.
4. **Check in daily** for the first two weeks, then weekly.
5. **Measure:** tasks completed, eligibility checked before visits, PA turnaround, and errors caught.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- **Handing over everything at once.** Start with two or three tasks and add more as procedures settle.
- **No written procedures.** Assistants can only follow the process you've written down; undocumented "tribal knowledge" leads to errors.
- **Shared logins.** Every person needs their own account so access can be audited and removed.
- **No single point of contact.** Name one person in the office who answers the assistant's questions and reviews their work.

This site is operated by Alliance Global Solutions, which provides remote staff. It signs a BAA with each client before any of its staff access protected health information. You can read about its [administrative virtual assistants](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/administrative/) or [browse virtual staff profiles](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistants/). To talk through which tasks to hand off, request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/).

**Approved vendor:** [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), which operates this site, provides dedicated remote staff for this work and signs a business associate agreement with each client before any PHI access. See [approved vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/) and [how we vet vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-we-vet-vendors/).

## Technology

Virtual medical assistants often work with scheduling automation, reminder systems and AI assistants that help draft messages or summarize inbox items for a person to review. Any tool that touches PHI should be approved by your practice and covered by a BAA where the tool vendor handles PHI ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

## Related guides

- [Revenue cycle management staffing (main guide)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)
- [Prior authorization specialist role](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/)
- [Credentialing specialist role](https://medicalbillingteam.com/credentialing-specialist/)
- [virtual medical receptionist services](https://medicalbillingteam.com/virtual-medical-receptionist/)

## FAQ

### What does a virtual medical assistant do?

Remote administrative work such as appointment reminders, eligibility checks, prior authorization follow-up, data and charge entry, payment posting support, and inbox and fax triage.

### Can a virtual medical assistant do clinical tasks?

No. Virtual administrative assistants shouldn't perform clinical tasks, triage or give medical advice. Keep those with licensed, in-person staff.

### Is a virtual medical assistant HIPAA compliant?

A virtual assistant can work within HIPAA when there's a BAA, secure access, minimum necessary permissions and training. There is no official HIPAA certification for assistants or companies.

### How is a virtual medical assistant different from a medical biller?

A virtual assistant handles broad administrative tasks; a biller focuses on claims, A/R and denials. Many small practices start with an assistant and add billing capacity later.

### How do I start with a virtual medical assistant?

List the most time-consuming administrative tasks, write procedures for two or three of them, agree on a schedule, sign a BAA, and check in daily for the first two weeks.

# Virtual medical receptionist: what the role covers and how to set it up

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** A virtual medical receptionist is a remote staff member who answers and returns patient calls, schedules and confirms appointments, updates demographics and insurance details, and routes messages, working in your phone system and practice management software. Unlike a generic answering service, a dedicated virtual receptionist learns your schedule rules and scripts. Because the role handles patient information, set up a BAA and secure access first.

Front-desk phones are where small practices feel staffing gaps first: missed calls, long holds and staff pulled away from patients in the office. A virtual medical receptionist can take that load off. This guide explains what the role does, what it shouldn't do, and how to set it up. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series, because accurate front-desk data is where clean claims start.

## What a virtual medical receptionist does

- **Inbound calls:** answer, identify the caller's need and resolve or route it using your scripts.
- **Scheduling:** book, reschedule and cancel appointments following your template rules (visit types, providers, durations).
- **Confirmations and reminders:** call or message patients ahead of visits and work the waitlist.
- **Demographics and insurance capture:** collect and update address, phone and insurance details before the visit, so [insurance verification](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/) can happen in advance.
- **Messages:** take and route messages for clinical staff (non-clinical intake only), refill requests per your protocol, and records requests.
- **Overflow and after-hours coverage** if you schedule it.
- **Billing questions:** basic balance questions and payment-plan setup per your scripts, with escalation to billing.

## What to keep with licensed or in-office staff

- Clinical triage, symptoms assessment or medical advice
- Emergencies: your phone tree and scripts should direct emergencies to 911 and urgent issues to clinical staff
- In-person tasks such as check-in and collecting payments at the desk
- Exceptions to financial policy (the receptionist prepares them; a manager approves)

## Virtual receptionist vs answering service vs virtual assistant

| | Answering service | Virtual medical receptionist | Virtual medical assistant |
|---|---|---|---|
| Works in your scheduling system | Usually not | Yes | Yes |
| Dedicated to your practice | Usually shared | Yes | Yes |
| Typical scope | Take messages | Calls, scheduling, intake data | Broader admin: eligibility, PA, data entry |
| Best for | After-hours messages | Phone volume and scheduling | Admin backlog beyond phones |

See also our guide to [virtual medical assistants](https://medicalbillingteam.com/virtual-medical-assistant/).

## Setting up the role

1. **Phones:** route calls to the receptionist through your phone system (queues, overflow rules, caller ID). Make sure call recording, if used, follows your policies and state law.
2. **Scripts:** greetings, common requests, scheduling rules, what to escalate and how, and emergency wording.
3. **Access:** a unique login to your scheduling/practice management system with only the permissions the role needs.
4. **Hours:** decide whether the receptionist covers core hours, overflow, lunch or after-hours.
5. **Quality:** review a sample of calls and scheduling accuracy weekly at first.
6. **Measures:** answer rate, average hold time, abandoned calls, appointments booked and no-show rate trends.

## HIPAA and security

A virtual receptionist hears and records patient information on every call. Before day one:

- sign a BAA with the staffing provider ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html));
- use unique logins with MFA and secure remote access;
- follow minimum necessary access, so the role sees scheduling and demographics but not full charts unless required;
- train on HIPAA and your identity-verification steps for callers; and
- block local downloads and personal devices.

Alliance Global Solutions signs a business associate agreement (BAA) with each client before any of its staff access protected health information. No receptionist or company is "HIPAA certified," because no official certification exists. Ask about specific safeguards using our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/).

## Getting help

It provides remote staff, including [call center and customer service staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/call-center-customer-service/) and [administrative virtual assistants](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/administrative/). To talk through phone coverage, [request help](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/); your request may be referred to Alliance Global Solutions.

**Approved vendor:** [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), which operates this site, provides dedicated remote staff for this work and signs a business associate agreement with each client before any PHI access. See [approved vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/) and [how we vet vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-we-vet-vendors/).

## Technology

Many practices pair a virtual receptionist with automated reminders, online scheduling and AI call or chat tools for after-hours triage, with staff handling anything the tools can't. If a phone or chat vendor handles PHI on your behalf, it generally needs a BAA ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

## FAQ

### What does a virtual medical receptionist do?

Answers and returns patient calls, schedules and confirms appointments, updates demographics and insurance details, routes non-clinical messages, and can cover overflow or after-hours calls, working in your systems.

### How is a virtual receptionist different from an answering service?

An answering service usually takes messages for many clients. A dedicated virtual medical receptionist works in your scheduling system, follows your scripts and handles scheduling and intake.

### Can a virtual receptionist handle clinical questions?

No. Clinical triage and medical advice stay with licensed staff. Scripts should route urgent issues to clinical staff and emergencies to 911.

### Is a virtual medical receptionist HIPAA compliant?

The role can work within HIPAA with a BAA, secure access, minimum necessary permissions and training. There is no official HIPAA certification for receptionists or companies.

### What should I measure?

Answer rate, hold time, abandoned calls, appointments booked, scheduling accuracy and no-show trends.

# Medical billing outsourcing: three models and how to choose

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** There are three main ways to outsource medical billing. A full-service billing company runs the whole function, usually for a percentage of collections. A staffing model gives you dedicated remote billers who work in your systems under your direction. A hybrid outsources specific queues, such as A/R or prior authorization. The right choice depends on how much control you want, your volume and your specialty.

"Outsourcing medical billing" can mean very different arrangements. Comparing a percentage-of-collections billing company with a dedicated remote biller is like comparing a managed service with a hire. This guide lays out the models so you can compare them fairly. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

## Model 1: Full-service billing company

The billing company takes over most or all of the revenue cycle: charge entry, claims, payment posting, A/R, denials and often patient statements. It usually works in its own software or yours.

- **Typical pricing:** a percentage of collections, a per-claim fee or a flat monthly fee
- **Good fit:** practices that want billing off their plate entirely
- **Watch for:** less visibility into day-to-day work, contract terms that make leaving hard, unclear ownership of data and reports, and fees on collections the practice would have received anyway

## Model 2: Dedicated remote staff (staffing model)

A staffing provider recruits and employs billers who work only on your account, in your systems, following your procedures. You direct the work; the provider handles employment, equipment, backup coverage and HR.

- **Typical pricing:** a monthly or hourly rate per full-time person
- **Good fit:** practices and billing companies that want control and visibility, and have someone to direct the work
- **Watch for:** you still need management time and documented procedures; quality depends on hiring and training

## Model 3: Hybrid

Keep billing in-house and outsource specific queues: A/R follow-up, denials, eligibility, prior authorization or credentialing. This works well when one area is chronically behind.

- **Typical pricing:** per person, per task or per queue
- **Good fit:** practices with a capable in-house biller who is overloaded
- **Watch for:** clear handoffs between teams so nothing falls through the gaps

## How to compare the models

| Factor | Billing company | Dedicated remote staff | Hybrid |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who directs the work | Vendor | You | Both |
| Software | Vendor's or yours | Yours | Yours |
| Pricing basis | % of collections or per claim | Per person | Per person or task |
| Visibility | Vendor reports | Your queues and reports | Mixed |
| Management time needed | Low | Medium | Medium |
| Exit difficulty | Contract-dependent | Usually simpler | Usually simpler |

Run your own numbers with the worksheet in our [staffing cost guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/). It uses public BLS wage and benefit data for the in-house baseline.

## Questions to ask any outsourcing partner

1. Who exactly will work on our account, and where are they located?
2. Will you sign a business associate agreement, and do your subcontractors sign one too?
3. What access controls do you use (MFA, secure remote access, no local downloads)?
4. What reports will we get, and can we see the work queues directly?
5. How are errors, write-offs and refunds approved?
6. What happens to our data and reports if we end the relationship?
7. What are the contract term, notice period and fees for leaving?
8. Can you give references we can contact directly?

Be cautious of anyone who promises a specific reduction in denials or A/R days before reviewing your data. Results depend on your payers, specialty and processes.

## HIPAA applies to every model

Any outsourcing partner whose people access patient information on your behalf is generally a business associate under HIPAA, and you need a BAA before access ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). There is no official "HIPAA certification" for vendors. Ask about specific safeguards instead, using our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/). If the team is overseas, read our guide to [offshore medical billers](https://medicalbillingteam.com/offshore-medical-billers/).

## Which model fits?

- **Small practice, no billing manager, wants it handled:** a billing company is often simplest.
- **Practice or billing company with a manager and growing volume:** dedicated remote staff gives capacity with control.
- **Strong in-house biller, one area behind:** hybrid.

This site is operated by Alliance Global Solutions, which offers the dedicated-staff model. It signs a BAA with each client before any of its staff access protected health information. You can read about its [outsourced medical billing staffing](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/) and broader [staffing services](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/services/). If you'd like help deciding, request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/); we'll tell you if a billing company is the better fit.

**Approved vendor:** [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), which operates this site, provides dedicated remote staff for this work and signs a business associate agreement with each client before any PHI access. See [approved vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/) and [how we vet vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-we-vet-vendors/).

## Technology

Whichever outsourcing model you choose, ask which tools touch your data: practice management, clearinghouse, eligibility automation and any AI assistants. Each tool vendor that handles PHI on your behalf is generally a business associate and needs a BAA ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

## Related guides

- [Revenue cycle management staffing (main guide)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)
- [Offshore medical billers: pros, cons and safeguards](https://medicalbillingteam.com/offshore-medical-billers/)
- [Hiring remote and offshore medical billers](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hire-remote-medical-billers/)
- [the full revenue cycle explained](https://medicalbillingteam.com/what-is-revenue-cycle-management/)

- [behavioral health billing services](https://medicalbillingteam.com/behavioral-health-billing/)
- [denial management services](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/)

## FAQ

### What does it cost to outsource medical billing?

Billing companies commonly charge a percentage of collections, per claim or a flat fee. Dedicated remote staff are usually priced per full-time person. Compare total cost, including your management time, with a worksheet.

### Is outsourcing medical billing HIPAA compliant?

It can be, when the partner signs a BAA and uses appropriate safeguards. HIPAA compliance depends on contracts and practices, not a certification; there is no official HIPAA certification.

### What is the difference between a billing company and a staffing model?

A billing company runs the function and directs the work. With a staffing model, dedicated remote billers work in your systems under your direction.

### Can I outsource only part of my billing?

Yes. A hybrid model outsources specific queues such as A/R follow-up, denials, eligibility, prior authorization or credentialing.

### Will outsourcing reduce my denials?

It depends on your payers, specialty, documentation and processes. Be cautious of promises of a specific reduction made before anyone reviews your data.

# Offshore medical billers: pros, cons and the safeguards to require

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** Offshore medical billing uses billers based outside the US. Offshore medical billers can add capacity at a lower hourly cost than local hires, and many practices and billing companies use them for A/R follow-up, eligibility, payment posting and denials. HIPAA doesn't ban offshore work, but HHS notes that overseas arrangements can raise risk and enforceability questions. Check your payer and Medicaid contracts, require a BAA and strong access controls, and include offshore access in your risk analysis.

Offshore billing teams are common in US healthcare, and they're also a source of understandable worry about data security, quality and communication. This guide covers where offshore billers fit, the real risks and the safeguards to require. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

## Why practices and billing companies go offshore

- **Hiring difficulty.** In a 2025 vendor survey, 38% of billing professionals said they struggle to find qualified candidates, and 28% cited unaffordable wages ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)).
- **Cost structure.** US billing and posting clerks had a median wage of $23.32 an hour in May 2025 ([BLS](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ocwage.t01.htm)), before benefits, which average 30% of private-industry compensation costs ([BLS](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ecec.nr0.htm)). Offshore staff are typically priced lower per hour, but compare total cost with our [staffing cost worksheet](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/).
- **Coverage.** A dedicated offshore person can keep queues moving when local staff are out, and some schedules cover hours your office doesn't.

## Work that suits offshore billers

- A/R follow-up and claim status checks
- Eligibility and benefits verification
- Payment posting and reconciliation
- Denial follow-up and corrected claims
- Charge entry from structured source documents
- Prior authorization submissions and follow-up (see [prior authorization specialist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/))

Work that needs physical presence, such as front-desk check-in, collecting payments in person or handling paper mail, stays local.

## The risks, honestly

- **Data security.** Offshore staff access PHI from outside the US. HHS's cloud computing guidance notes that HIPAA doesn't prohibit storing or processing PHI overseas, but that doing so may raise the risks to the data and can make legal enforcement harder; covered entities should consider these risks in their risk analysis ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html)).
- **Contract restrictions.** Some payer contracts, state Medicaid programs and government plans restrict offshore access to member data. Check yours before you start.
- **Quality and communication.** Billing depends on payer-specific knowledge and clear notes. Poor hiring or training shows up quickly in denials.
- **Time zones.** Payer phone lines keep US hours. Confirm schedules in writing.

## Safeguards to require

1. **Business associate agreement** with the provider before any access, and subcontractor BAAs where applicable ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)).
2. **Unique logins and MFA** on every system.
3. **Secure remote access** through a virtual desktop or VPN, so PHI stays in your environment.
4. **No local downloads, printing, screenshots or USB storage**, technically enforced where possible.
5. **Company-managed, encrypted devices** and secured work locations.
6. **Role-based, minimum necessary access**, removed the same day someone leaves.
7. **HIPAA training** at onboarding and annually, with records.
8. **Background checks** and a clear acceptable-use policy.
9. **Incident response** with a defined, prompt notification timeline. Under HIPAA, a business associate must notify the covered entity of a breach without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/breach-notification/index.html)). Many contracts set a shorter window.

And remember there's no official "HIPAA certification." Ask for evidence of the safeguards above instead. Our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/) has 15 questions to ask.

## Start small

Start with one well-defined queue, such as eligibility or A/R follow-up, with written procedures and daily spot checks. Review results after 30 days before expanding. Our guide to [hiring remote medical billers](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hire-remote-medical-billers/) includes interview questions and a 30-day onboarding plan.

## Offshore vs nearshore vs US remote

| | Offshore | Nearshore | US remote |
|---|---|---|---|
| Typical hourly cost | Lowest | Middle | Highest |
| Time-zone overlap | Needs scheduling | Good | Full |
| Contract restrictions | Check carefully | Check | Usually fewer |
| HIPAA safeguards needed | Same, plus overseas risk analysis | Same, plus cross-border review | Same |

It signs a BAA with each client before any of its staff access protected health information. You can read about its [offshore medical billing staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/). ## Technology

Offshore teams often use the same automation as onshore teams: eligibility bots, claim scrubbers and AI assistants. Any tool that stores or processes PHI, wherever it is hosted, needs a BAA when the tool vendor handles PHI on your behalf ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. - [Medical billing outsourcing: three models](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-outsourcing/)
- [Hiring remote medical coders](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hire-remote-medical-coders/)

## FAQ

### Is offshore medical billing legal under HIPAA?

HIPAA doesn't prohibit offshore work. HHS notes overseas arrangements may raise risk and enforcement challenges, so include them in your risk analysis, sign a BAA and check payer and Medicaid contracts for restrictions.

### What billing tasks can offshore staff do?

Common tasks include A/R follow-up, eligibility verification, payment posting, denial follow-up, charge entry and prior authorization submissions.

### How do offshore billers keep PHI secure?

Through a BAA, unique logins with MFA, secure remote access via virtual desktop or VPN, no local downloads or printing, managed encrypted devices, role-based access, training and incident response.

### Do offshore billers work US hours?

Many teams work schedules that overlap US business hours so they can call payers. Confirm the schedule in writing.

### Are offshore medical billers HIPAA certified?

No one is. There is no official HIPAA certification; HHS does not certify vendors. Ask for evidence of specific safeguards instead.

# Denial management basics: a practical guide for practices and billing teams

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** Denial management means tracking every denied claim, then correcting and resubmitting it or appealing it before the deadline, and feeding the root cause back to the front desk, coders and providers so it doesn't happen again. It works best with one owner, a single queue sorted by payer and reason, and a fixed weekly routine.

Every practice gets denials. The difference between practices that lose revenue to them and practices that don't is usually not software. It's whether someone owns the denial queue, works it on a schedule and fixes the causes upstream. This guide covers the basics and where staffing fits in. It is part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

## Why denials deserve a dedicated owner

Public data show how common denials are. KFF's analysis of federal transparency data found HealthCare.gov insurers denied 20% of in-network claims in 2023 ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/private-insurance/claims-denials-and-appeals-in-aca-marketplace-plans-in-2023/)). That covers one market segment, but the pattern is familiar to anyone who works claims. In a 2025 vendor survey of billing professionals, 40% reported that denials had increased over the previous year ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)).

When nobody owns denials, they age quietly in a work queue until the appeal window closes.

## Rejections vs denials

- **Rejection:** the claim never entered the payer's adjudication system, usually because of a data or formatting error (wrong member ID format, missing NPI, invalid code). Fix and resubmit quickly. Rejections don't usually carry appeal rights because no decision was made.
- **Denial:** the payer processed the claim and refused payment in whole or part. The remittance carries claim adjustment reason codes (CARCs) and often remittance advice remark codes (RARCs) explaining why. These are standard code sets used by all payers, as CMS describes in its Medicare Claims Processing Manual ([CMS, Ch. 1](https://www.cms.gov/regulations-and-guidance/guidance/manuals/downloads/clm104c01.pdf)).

## Common root causes

The same vendor survey asked billers about top denial reasons ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)):

- coordination of benefits issues (45% of respondents);
- non-coverage (39%);
- prior authorization and referral issues (31%);
- timely filing errors (26%);
- inaccurate patient demographic information (25%).

In KFF's federal data, insurers cited administrative reasons for 21% of in-network denials and lack of prior authorization or referral for 9%, while the largest category was "Other" at 34% ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/private-insurance/claims-denials-and-appeals-in-aca-marketplace-plans-in-2023/)).

Most of these trace back to the **front end**: eligibility checks, demographics capture and authorizations. That's why denial management and [eligibility and prior authorization](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/) work belong together.

## A simple denial workflow

### 1. Capture every denial

Make sure denials from ERAs (835s), paper EOBs and payer portals all land in one queue. Payment posters are often the first to see a denial; they should flag it, not just post a zero.

### 2. Categorize

Tag each denial by payer, reason code group (eligibility, authorization, coding, timely filing, medical necessity, duplicate, bundling, other) and whether it is **preventable**.

### 3. Prioritize

Sort by appeal or corrected-claim deadline first, then dollar value. A small denial with a deadline next week beats a large one with three months left.

### 4. Act

- **Correct and resubmit** for fixable data errors (demographics, codes, modifiers).
- **Appeal** when the claim was correct and the payer was wrong. Use the payer's form, cite the policy, attach documentation, and track the appeal date.
- **Bill the right party** for coordination of benefits issues.
- **Write off** only under your written write-off policy, with approval.

### 5. Track and close the loop

Log the outcome. Each month, review the top preventable reasons by payer and send fixes upstream: a front-desk script change, an authorization rule, a coding education note.

## Appeals: the basics

- Read the denial reason and the payer's policy before writing anything.
- Know the deadline. Payer appeal windows differ, and Medicare has its own multi-level appeals process.
- Include what the payer needs: claim details, the specific reason you disagree, policy citations and supporting documentation.
- Follow up. An appeal that's never tracked is an appeal that's lost.

Appeals can succeed. KFF reports that among Medicare Advantage prior authorization denials in 2023 that were appealed, 81.7% were fully or partially overturned, yet only 11.7% of denials were appealed (cited in [AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/fixing-prior-auth-nearly-40-prior-authorizations-week-way)). That's prior authorization data, not claims, but it shows the value of persistence.

## Denial KPIs to track

- **Denial rate:** denied claims (or dollars) ÷ claims (or dollars) submitted, by payer and reason.
- **Preventable denial share:** denials in categories the practice controls.
- **Days to work a denial:** from receipt to first action.
- **Overturn rate:** successful appeals ÷ appeals filed.
- **Denial write-offs:** dollars written off due to denials, per month.

We don't publish a universal "good" denial rate, because public benchmarks vary by specialty and methodology. Trend your own numbers. Our [RCM KPI definitions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) explain how to calculate each one consistently.

## Who should do denial work?

Denial work needs someone with payer knowledge, coding familiarity, patience on the phone and protected time. Options:

- **Your existing biller**, if they actually have the hours. Often they don't.
- **A dedicated denial management specialist**, in-house or remote, who works the queue daily.
- **An outsourced billing company** that includes appeals in its scope (confirm this; some don't).

A remote denial specialist works in your billing system and payer portals under your rules and write-off policy. If you're considering that route, read our [guide to hiring remote medical billers](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hire-remote-medical-billers/) and make sure HIPAA safeguards are in place first ([HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/)).

## Preventing denials upstream

- Verify eligibility and benefits before every visit, not just new patients.
- Confirm authorization requirements by payer and service, and track expirations and visit limits.
- Capture demographics and insurance cards accurately; re-verify at every visit.
- Scrub claims before submission and fix rejections daily.
- Give coders feedback on recurring coding denials.
- Track timely filing deadlines per payer.

This site is operated by [Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/), a provider of remote billing staff. If your denial queue is growing faster than your team can work it, you can [contact the company directly](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/contact/) or request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/) here.

## A weekly denial routine for small teams

If you only have a few hours a week for denials, a fixed routine keeps them from piling up:

1. **Monday:** pull new denials from ERAs and the clearinghouse into one list. Tag each by payer, reason code and dollar amount.
2. **Tuesday-Wednesday:** correct and resubmit the quick fixes (demographics, coding errors, missing modifiers) and call payers on the unclear ones.
3. **Thursday:** draft appeals for high-dollar or recurring denials, with supporting documentation and the payer's appeal deadline noted.
4. **Friday:** review the week. What were the top three reasons? Which could the front desk, providers or coders prevent? Send one short note to the people who can fix the cause.

Keep the list in a shared tracker so nothing depends on one person's memory.

**Approved vendor:** [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), which operates this site, provides dedicated remote staff for this work and signs a business associate agreement with each client before any PHI access. See [approved vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/) and [how we vet vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-we-vet-vendors/).

## Denial code guides

Most denials trace back to a handful of CARC codes. Each guide covers what the code means, common causes and a fix-and-prevent checklist:

- [CO-16: claim lacks information or has billing errors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-16/)
- [CO-22: coordination of benefits denials](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-22/)
- [CO-29: timely filing limit expired](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-29/)
- [CO-97: bundled or included services](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-97/)
- [CO-197: missing precertification or authorization](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-197/)
- [CO-204: service not covered under the patient's plan](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-204/)

## Technology

Denial management is shifting upstream into denial prevention: claim scrubbing, denial-prediction models and payer-policy checks before care is delivered ([Fierce Healthcare](https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/health-tech/thoreau-backed-ensemble-penelope-health-partner-tackle-payer-denials-upstream)). Remits use standard X12 group and reason codes, so denials can be sorted automatically into work queues ([X12](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes)). People still write appeals and fix root causes. Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

## Related guides

- [How to reduce A/R days](https://medicalbillingteam.com/reduce-ar-days/)
- [Eligibility verification and prior authorization](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/)
- [Revenue cycle management staffing (main guide)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)

## FAQ

### What is the difference between a claim rejection and a denial?

A rejection means the claim was not accepted for processing, usually because of formatting or data errors caught by the clearinghouse or payer front end. A denial means the payer processed the claim and decided not to pay all or part of it. Rejections are corrected and resubmitted; denials are corrected, resubmitted or appealed.

### What are the most common causes of claim denials?

Common categories include eligibility and coordination of benefits problems, non-covered services, missing prior authorization or referral, timely filing, coding errors and inaccurate patient demographics. In one 2025 vendor survey, billers most often cited coordination of benefits, non-coverage and prior authorization issues.

### How often should denials be worked?

Daily or at least weekly, prioritized by dollar value and appeal deadline. Denials left for weeks risk missing appeal windows.

### What is a good denial rate?

Benchmarks vary by specialty, payer mix and how the rate is calculated. Track your own denial rate by payer and reason each month and focus on the reasons you can prevent.

### Should denial work be in-house or outsourced?

Either can work. What matters is that a specific person owns the queue, has payer knowledge and time to do it, and feeds root causes back to the front desk and coders.

# CO-16 denial code: meaning, causes and fixes

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** CO-16 means the payer couldn't process the claim or line because information was missing or there was a submission or billing error. X12 defines CARC 16 as "Claim/service lacks information or has submission/billing error(s)." The fix is in the remark code (RARC) that must accompany it: it tells you exactly what's missing. Correct that item and resubmit, usually as a corrected or new claim per the payer's rules.

This guide explains denial code CO-16: the official definition, what usually causes it, how to fix it and how to prevent it. It's part of our [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/) guide and the [denial code guides](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/#denial-code-guides) series.

## Official definition (X12 CARC 16)

Claim adjustment reason codes (CARCs) are maintained by X12 and describe "why a claim or service line was paid differently than it was billed." CARC 16 reads:

> "Claim/service lacks information or has submission/billing error(s)."

Source: [X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes), checked October 18, 2026. X12 adds that at least one Remark Code must be provided with CARC 16 (a Remittance Advice Remark Code, or RARC, or an NCPDP reject reason), and that the code should not be used for claims attachments or other documentation.

## What the "CO" prefix means

The letters before the number are a claim adjustment **group code**. X12 says group codes "generally assign responsibility for the adjustment amounts" and defines them as CO (Contractual Obligation), PR (Patient Responsibility), OA (Other Adjustment) and PI (Payer Initiated Reductions) ([X12](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes)). With CO, the adjustment is generally treated as the provider's responsibility under its payer contract rather than the patient's, so check your contract before billing the patient for a CO amount. The same reason code can appear with a different group code (for example PR or OA), which changes who is responsible.

## Common causes

- Missing or invalid patient demographics (name, date of birth, member ID mismatch)
- Missing or invalid provider identifiers (rendering, referring or billing NPI; taxonomy)
- Missing or invalid diagnosis pointer, place of service or modifier
- Missing information the payer requires for that service (for example, units, dates, NDC for drugs)
- Missing prior-payer information on a secondary claim
- Formatting errors that passed the clearinghouse but failed payer edits

## How to fix it

1. Read the RARC(s) on the remittance first; CO-16 alone doesn't say what's missing.
2. Fix the specific field in the practice management system so it doesn't recur on future claims.
3. Resubmit as the payer instructs (many treat CO-16 as a correct-and-resubmit, not an appeal).
4. Track resubmission against the payer's timely filing limit.
5. Log the RARC and root cause so the front desk, coders or charge entry can prevent it.

## How to prevent it

- Scrub claims for required fields before submission
- Verify demographics and insurance at every visit
- Keep provider NPI/taxonomy data current with each payer (see [credentialing services](https://medicalbillingteam.com/credentialing-services/))
- Build payer-specific edits for frequent RARCs

## Who should work these denials

Denials need an owner with payer knowledge and time to follow up before deadlines. See [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/) and [what an AR specialist does](https://medicalbillingteam.com/ar-specialist/). If your team doesn't have the capacity, you can [request help](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/); requests may be referred to [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), which operates this site and is currently our only [approved vendor](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/). For A/R follow-up and denial rework capacity, see its [remote accounting staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/accounting/) page.

*This guide is general information, not coding or legal advice. Payer rules vary; check the payer's policy and the remark codes on your remittance.*

## Technology

Claim scrubbers and billing automation can catch many missing or invalid data errors before a claim goes out, and denial-prediction tools flag claims that payers have rejected for CO-16 in the past. Group and reason codes come from the standard X12 code list, so remits can be routed automatically to the right work queue ([X12](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes)). A person still has to fix the underlying cause and resubmit or appeal. Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

## Related guides

- [Denial management (hub)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/)
- [CO-22: coordination of benefits](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-22/)
- [CO-197: authorization absent](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-197/)
- [What is revenue cycle management?](https://medicalbillingteam.com/what-is-revenue-cycle-management/)
- [CO-29 timely filing denials](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-29/)

## FAQ

### What does denial code CO-16 mean?

X12 defines CARC 16 as "Claim/service lacks information or has submission/billing error(s)." With group code CO, the adjustment is generally the provider's responsibility under its contract.

### How do I find out what's missing on a CO-16 denial?

Look at the remark code (RARC) on the remittance. X12 requires at least one remark code with CARC 16, and it identifies the missing or invalid information.

### Should I appeal a CO-16 denial?

Usually not. CO-16 is typically corrected and resubmitted. Follow the payer's corrected-claim rules and watch the timely filing limit.

### Can I bill the patient for a CO-16 adjustment?

Generally no. CO indicates a contractual obligation rather than patient responsibility. Fix and resubmit the claim instead.

### How do I prevent CO-16 denials?

Scrub claims for required fields, verify demographics and insurance at every visit, keep provider identifiers current with payers, and track recurring remark codes.

# CO-22 denial code: meaning, causes and fixes

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** CO-22 means the payer believes another plan should pay first under coordination of benefits (COB). X12 defines CARC 22 as "This care may be covered by another payer per coordination of benefits." To fix it, confirm the patient's other coverage and which plan is primary, update the payer and your system, bill the primary first, then send the secondary claim with the primary's payment information.

This guide explains denial code CO-22: the official definition, what usually causes it, how to fix it and how to prevent it. It's part of our [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/) guide and the [denial code guides](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/#denial-code-guides) series.

## Official definition (X12 CARC 22)

Claim adjustment reason codes (CARCs) are maintained by X12 and describe "why a claim or service line was paid differently than it was billed." CARC 22 reads:

> "This care may be covered by another payer per coordination of benefits."

Source: [X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes), checked October 18, 2026. 

## What the "CO" prefix means

The letters before the number are a claim adjustment **group code**. X12 says group codes "generally assign responsibility for the adjustment amounts" and defines them as CO (Contractual Obligation), PR (Patient Responsibility), OA (Other Adjustment) and PI (Payer Initiated Reductions) ([X12](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes)). With CO, the adjustment is generally treated as the provider's responsibility under its payer contract rather than the patient's, so check your contract before billing the patient for a CO amount. The same reason code can appear with a different group code (for example PR or OA), which changes who is responsible.

## Common causes

- The patient has other coverage (spouse's plan, employer plan, Medicare, Medicaid) that the payer lists as primary
- The payer's COB record is outdated or incomplete
- The patient didn't report other coverage at registration
- Medicare Secondary Payer situations (for example, employer coverage or liability) not identified
- The secondary claim was sent without the primary's remittance information

## How to fix it

1. Ask the patient about all current coverage and confirm which plan is primary (birthday rule, employment status, Medicare rules as applicable).
2. Have the patient update their COB information with the payer if the payer's record is wrong; many payers require the member to do this.
3. Bill the primary payer first.
4. Send the secondary claim with the primary payment and adjustment details.
5. Track the claim against timely filing limits while COB is being resolved.

## How to prevent it

- Ask about other coverage at every registration, not just new patients
- Use eligibility responses to spot other-coverage flags before the visit (see [insurance verification services](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/))
- Update COB order in your system as soon as it changes
- Train front-desk and [virtual receptionist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/virtual-medical-receptionist/) scripts to ask the COB questions

## Who should work these denials

Denials need an owner with payer knowledge and time to follow up before deadlines. See [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/) and [what an AR specialist does](https://medicalbillingteam.com/ar-specialist/). If your team doesn't have the capacity, you can [request help](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/); requests may be referred to [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), which operates this site and is currently our only [approved vendor](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/). For A/R follow-up and denial rework capacity, see its [remote accounting staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/accounting/) page.

*This guide is general information, not coding or legal advice. Payer rules vary; check the payer's policy and the remark codes on your remittance.*

## Technology

Claim scrubbers and billing automation can catch many coordination-of-benefits problems through up-front eligibility checks before a claim goes out, and denial-prediction tools flag claims that payers have rejected for CO-22 in the past. Group and reason codes come from the standard X12 code list, so remits can be routed automatically to the right work queue ([X12](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes)). A person still has to fix the underlying cause and resubmit or appeal. Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

## Related guides

- [Denial management (hub)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/)
- [CO-16: missing information](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-16/)
- [CO-204: not covered under the plan](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-204/)
- [What is revenue cycle management?](https://medicalbillingteam.com/what-is-revenue-cycle-management/)
- [CO-29 timely filing denials](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-29/)

## FAQ

### What does denial code CO-22 mean?

X12 defines CARC 22 as "This care may be covered by another payer per coordination of benefits." The payer thinks another plan should pay first.

### How do I fix a CO-22 denial?

Confirm the patient's other coverage and primary order, have the payer's COB record updated if needed, bill the primary first, then send the secondary claim with the primary's payment details.

### Who updates coordination of benefits with the insurer?

Often the member must update COB directly with their plan. Your staff can explain what's needed and resubmit once it's updated.

### Are COB denials common?

In a 2025 vendor survey of billing professionals, coordination of benefits was the most commonly cited denial reason, named by 45% of respondents.

### How do I prevent CO-22 denials?

Ask about other coverage at every visit, review eligibility responses for other-coverage flags, and keep COB order current in your system.

# CO-29 denial code: meaning, causes and fixes

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** CO-29 means the claim was received after the payer's filing deadline. X12 defines CARC 29 as "The time limit for filing has expired." For Medicare, the limit is one calendar year from the date of service. If you have proof the claim was filed on time (clearinghouse acceptance reports, prior submissions), appeal with that proof. Otherwise the amount is usually written off, so prevention matters most.

This guide explains denial code CO-29: the official definition, what usually causes it, how to fix it and how to prevent it. It's part of our [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/) guide and the [denial code guides](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/#denial-code-guides) series.

## Official definition (X12 CARC 29)

Claim adjustment reason codes (CARCs) are maintained by X12 and describe "why a claim or service line was paid differently than it was billed." CARC 29 reads:

> "The time limit for filing has expired."

Source: [X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes), checked October 18, 2026. 

## What the "CO" prefix means

The letters before the number are a claim adjustment **group code**. X12 says group codes "generally assign responsibility for the adjustment amounts" and defines them as CO (Contractual Obligation), PR (Patient Responsibility), OA (Other Adjustment) and PI (Payer Initiated Reductions) ([X12](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes)). With CO, the adjustment is generally treated as the provider's responsibility under its payer contract rather than the patient's, so check your contract before billing the patient for a CO amount. The same reason code can appear with a different group code (for example PR or OA), which changes who is responsible.

## Common causes

- The claim was never submitted, or was rejected and never corrected
- A rejection at the clearinghouse wasn't noticed
- Coordination of benefits delays pushed the secondary claim past its limit
- Corrected claims were sent after the payer's corrected-claim deadline
- Credentialing delays held claims too long

## How to fix it

1. Gather proof of timely filing: clearinghouse acceptance reports, payer acknowledgment, or prior submission records.
2. Appeal with that proof if it exists, following the payer's process.
3. Check whether an exception applies (for example, retroactive eligibility or payer error).
4. If no proof or exception exists, write off as a contractual adjustment; don't bill the patient for a CO amount.
5. Log the root cause.

## How to prevent it

- Track filing limits for every major payer; Medicare's is one calendar year from the date of service ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/regulations-and-guidance/guidance/manuals/downloads/clm104c01.pdf))
- Work clearinghouse rejections daily
- Work A/R by age so claims don't sit (see [days in AR](https://medicalbillingteam.com/reduce-ar-days/))
- Hold claims for credentialing only with a plan and a deadline

## Who should work these denials

Denials need an owner with payer knowledge and time to follow up before deadlines. See [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/) and [what an AR specialist does](https://medicalbillingteam.com/ar-specialist/). If your team doesn't have the capacity, you can [request help](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/); requests may be referred to [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), which operates this site and is currently our only [approved vendor](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/). For A/R follow-up and denial rework capacity, see its [remote accounting staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/accounting/) page.

*This guide is general information, not coding or legal advice. Payer rules vary; check the payer's policy and the remark codes on your remittance.*

## Technology

Claim scrubbers and billing automation can catch many claims nearing the filing limit through timely-filing alerts before a claim goes out, and denial-prediction tools flag claims that payers have rejected for CO-29 in the past. Group and reason codes come from the standard X12 code list, so remits can be routed automatically to the right work queue ([X12](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes)). A person still has to fix the underlying cause and resubmit or appeal. Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

## Related guides

- [Denial management (hub)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/)
- [CO-16: missing information](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-16/)
- [CO-97: bundled services](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-97/)
- [What is revenue cycle management?](https://medicalbillingteam.com/what-is-revenue-cycle-management/)
- [CO-22 coordination of benefits](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-22/)

## FAQ

### What does denial code CO-29 mean?

X12 defines CARC 29 as "The time limit for filing has expired." The payer received the claim after its filing deadline.

### What is Medicare's timely filing limit?

CMS sets it at one calendar year from the date of service. Commercial payer limits vary by contract and are often shorter.

### Can a CO-29 denial be overturned?

Sometimes, if you can prove the claim was filed on time, for example with clearinghouse acceptance reports, or if an exception such as retroactive eligibility applies.

### Can I bill the patient for a timely filing denial?

Generally no. A CO adjustment indicates a contractual obligation rather than patient responsibility.

### How do I prevent CO-29 denials?

Track payer filing limits, work clearinghouse rejections daily, follow up on A/R by age, and keep COB and credentialing delays from holding claims too long.

# CO-97 denial code: meaning, causes and fixes

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** CO-97 means the payer considers the service bundled, meaning it's included in the payment for another service already processed. X12 defines CARC 97 as "The benefit for this service is included in the payment/allowance for another service/procedure that has already been adjudicated." Check payer bundling edits and documentation. If the service was truly separate and distinct, a correct modifier and supporting documentation may support a corrected claim or appeal.

This guide explains denial code CO-97: the official definition, what usually causes it, how to fix it and how to prevent it. It's part of our [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/) guide and the [denial code guides](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/#denial-code-guides) series.

## Official definition (X12 CARC 97)

Claim adjustment reason codes (CARCs) are maintained by X12 and describe "why a claim or service line was paid differently than it was billed." CARC 97 reads:

> "The benefit for this service is included in the payment/allowance for another service/procedure that has already been adjudicated."

Source: [X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes), checked October 18, 2026. 

## What the "CO" prefix means

The letters before the number are a claim adjustment **group code**. X12 says group codes "generally assign responsibility for the adjustment amounts" and defines them as CO (Contractual Obligation), PR (Patient Responsibility), OA (Other Adjustment) and PI (Payer Initiated Reductions) ([X12](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes)). With CO, the adjustment is generally treated as the provider's responsibility under its payer contract rather than the patient's, so check your contract before billing the patient for a CO amount. The same reason code can appear with a different group code (for example PR or OA), which changes who is responsible.

## Common causes

- The service is a component of another procedure billed on the same day
- Payer or national correct coding edits bundle the code pair
- A modifier indicating a separate, distinct service was missing or not supported
- The service was billed within a global period for a related procedure

## How to fix it

1. Identify which service it was bundled into (check the remittance and payer policy).
2. Review documentation: was the service separate and distinct?
3. If yes, correct the claim with the appropriate modifier per payer policy, or appeal with documentation.
4. If no, write the line off as a contractual adjustment; don't bill the patient for a CO amount.
5. Note payer-specific bundling rules for coders.

## How to prevent it

- Run code-pair edits before submission
- Train coders on modifier rules and payer policies (see [outsource medical coding](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hire-remote-medical-coders/))
- Audit modifier use regularly

## Who should work these denials

Denials need an owner with payer knowledge and time to follow up before deadlines. See [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/) and [what an AR specialist does](https://medicalbillingteam.com/ar-specialist/). If your team doesn't have the capacity, you can [request help](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/); requests may be referred to [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), which operates this site and is currently our only [approved vendor](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/). For A/R follow-up and denial rework capacity, see its [remote accounting staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/accounting/) page.

*This guide is general information, not coding or legal advice. Payer rules vary; check the payer's policy and the remark codes on your remittance.*

## Technology

Claim scrubbers and billing automation can catch many bundling and modifier conflicts through edit checks before a claim goes out, and denial-prediction tools flag claims that payers have rejected for CO-97 in the past. Group and reason codes come from the standard X12 code list, so remits can be routed automatically to the right work queue ([X12](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes)). A person still has to fix the underlying cause and resubmit or appeal. Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

## Related guides

- [Denial management (hub)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/)
- [CO-16: missing information](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-16/)
- [CO-29: timely filing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-29/)
- [What is revenue cycle management?](https://medicalbillingteam.com/what-is-revenue-cycle-management/)
- [CO-204 non-covered service denials](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-204/)

## FAQ

### What does denial code CO-97 mean?

X12 defines CARC 97 as "The benefit for this service is included in the payment/allowance for another service/procedure that has already been adjudicated." The service was bundled.

### How do I fix a CO-97 denial?

Find the service it was bundled into, review documentation, and if the service was separate and distinct, correct the claim with the appropriate modifier or appeal with documentation per payer policy.

### Should I add a modifier to every CO-97 line?

No. Use modifiers only when documentation supports a separate, distinct service. Unsupported modifier use creates compliance risk.

### Can I bill the patient for a bundled service?

Generally no. A CO adjustment indicates a contractual obligation rather than patient responsibility.

### How do I prevent CO-97 denials?

Run code-pair edits before submission, train coders on payer bundling and modifier rules, and audit modifier use.

# CO-197 denial code: meaning, causes and fixes

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** CO-197 means the payer found no required precertification, authorization, notification or pre-treatment approval for the service. X12 defines CARC 197 as "Precertification/authorization/notification/pre-treatment absent." First check whether an authorization actually exists and was left off the claim; if so, correct and resubmit. If none was obtained, ask about retro-authorization or appeal options, and fix the front-end process so it doesn't recur.

This guide explains denial code CO-197: the official definition, what usually causes it, how to fix it and how to prevent it. It's part of our [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/) guide and the [denial code guides](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/#denial-code-guides) series.

## Official definition (X12 CARC 197)

Claim adjustment reason codes (CARCs) are maintained by X12 and describe "why a claim or service line was paid differently than it was billed." CARC 197 reads:

> "Precertification/authorization/notification/pre-treatment absent."

Source: [X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes), checked October 18, 2026. 

## What the "CO" prefix means

The letters before the number are a claim adjustment **group code**. X12 says group codes "generally assign responsibility for the adjustment amounts" and defines them as CO (Contractual Obligation), PR (Patient Responsibility), OA (Other Adjustment) and PI (Payer Initiated Reductions) ([X12](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes)). With CO, the adjustment is generally treated as the provider's responsibility under its payer contract rather than the patient's, so check your contract before billing the patient for a CO amount. The same reason code can appear with a different group code (for example PR or OA), which changes who is responsible.

## Common causes

- No authorization was requested before the service
- An authorization exists but the number wasn't on the claim
- The authorization was for a different provider, location, date range or service
- Authorized units or visits were exceeded (X12 uses CARC 198 for 'exceeded')
- The authorization expired (CARC 302 covers an expired time limit)

## How to fix it

1. Search your records and the payer portal for an existing authorization.
2. If found, correct the claim with the authorization number and resubmit.
3. If the authorization covers a different provider or service, check CARCs 284 and 296, which X12 uses when an authorization number may be valid but doesn't apply.
4. If none exists, ask the payer about retro-authorization or appeal, with documentation of medical necessity and urgency.
5. Feed the miss back to the PA owner.

## How to prevent it

- Maintain a prior authorization matrix by payer and service
- Make authorization part of scheduling, not an afterthought
- Track units, visits and expirations (see [prior authorization specialist and outsourcing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/))
- Make sure authorization numbers flow onto claims automatically

## Who should work these denials

Denials need an owner with payer knowledge and time to follow up before deadlines. See [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/) and [what an AR specialist does](https://medicalbillingteam.com/ar-specialist/). If your team doesn't have the capacity, you can [request help](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/); requests may be referred to [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), which operates this site and is currently our only [approved vendor](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/). For A/R follow-up and denial rework capacity, see its [remote accounting staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/accounting/) page.

*This guide is general information, not coding or legal advice. Payer rules vary; check the payer's policy and the remark codes on your remittance.*

## Technology

Claim scrubbers and billing automation can catch many missing authorizations by matching scheduled services to authorization records before a claim goes out, and denial-prediction tools flag claims that payers have rejected for CO-197 in the past. Group and reason codes come from the standard X12 code list, so remits can be routed automatically to the right work queue ([X12](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes)). A person still has to fix the underlying cause and resubmit or appeal. Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

## Related guides

- [Denial management (hub)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/)
- [CO-204: not covered under the plan](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-204/)
- [CO-16: missing information](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-16/)
- [What is revenue cycle management?](https://medicalbillingteam.com/what-is-revenue-cycle-management/)
- [CO-29 timely filing denials](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-29/)

## FAQ

### What does denial code CO-197 mean?

X12 defines CARC 197 as "Precertification/authorization/notification/pre-treatment absent." The payer found no required authorization for the service.

### How do I fix a CO-197 denial?

Check for an existing authorization and correct the claim if one exists; otherwise ask the payer about retro-authorization or appeal with documentation.

### What is the difference between CARC 197 and 198?

X12 defines 197 as authorization absent and 198 as precertification, notification, authorization or pre-treatment exceeded.

### Are prior authorization denials worth appealing?

Often. KFF data cited by the AMA shows 81.7% of appealed Medicare Advantage PA denials in 2023 were fully or partially overturned, though only 11.7% were appealed.

### How do I prevent CO-197 denials?

Keep a PA matrix by payer and service, build authorization into scheduling, track units and expirations, and make sure authorization numbers reach the claim.
