# CO-204 denial code: meaning, causes and fixes

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** CO-204 means the service, equipment or drug isn't covered under the patient's current benefit plan. X12 defines CARC 204 as "This service/equipment/drug is not covered under the patient's current benefit plan." Check whether the plan really excludes the service, whether it was billed with the right codes, and whether a coverage exception or appeal applies. Prevent it by verifying benefits for the specific service before it's provided.

This guide explains denial code CO-204: the official definition, what usually causes it, how to fix it and how to prevent it. It's part of our [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/) guide and the [denial code guides](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/#denial-code-guides) series.

## Official definition (X12 CARC 204)

Claim adjustment reason codes (CARCs) are maintained by X12 and describe "why a claim or service line was paid differently than it was billed." CARC 204 reads:

> "This service/equipment/drug is not covered under the patient's current benefit plan"

Source: [X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes), checked October 18, 2026. 

## What the "CO" prefix means

The letters before the number are a claim adjustment **group code**. X12 says group codes "generally assign responsibility for the adjustment amounts" and defines them as CO (Contractual Obligation), PR (Patient Responsibility), OA (Other Adjustment) and PI (Payer Initiated Reductions) ([X12](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes)). With CO, the adjustment is generally treated as the provider's responsibility under its payer contract rather than the patient's, so check your contract before billing the patient for a CO amount. The same reason code can appear with a different group code (for example PR or OA), which changes who is responsible.

## Common causes

- The plan excludes the service (benefit exclusion)
- The service is covered only under a different benefit (for example, a carved-out behavioral health or pharmacy benefit)
- Coding doesn't reflect the covered service
- The patient changed plans and the new plan doesn't cover the service
- The service required a coverage exception that wasn't requested

## How to fix it

1. Confirm the exclusion with the payer and get the reference number.
2. Check coding: does a covered code accurately describe the service?
3. Check whether another benefit or administrator should receive the claim (carve-outs).
4. If clinically appropriate, ask about an exception or appeal process.
5. Before billing the patient, check your payer contract, any advance notice or waiver rules, and state law; CO generally indicates provider liability.

## How to prevent it

- Verify benefits for the specific service, not just active coverage
- Identify carve-outs during eligibility checks (see [treatment center VOB](https://medicalbillingteam.com/treatment-center-vob/))
- Give patients advance notice of non-covered services where your policies and payer rules allow

## Who should work these denials

Denials need an owner with payer knowledge and time to follow up before deadlines. See [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/) and [what an AR specialist does](https://medicalbillingteam.com/ar-specialist/). If your team doesn't have the capacity, you can [request help](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/); requests may be referred to [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), which operates this site and is currently our only [approved vendor](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/). For A/R follow-up and denial rework capacity, see its [remote accounting staff](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/accounting/) page.

*This guide is general information, not coding or legal advice. Payer rules vary; check the payer's policy and the remark codes on your remittance.*

## Technology

Claim scrubbers and billing automation can catch many non-covered services through benefit checks before a claim goes out, and denial-prediction tools flag claims that payers have rejected for CO-204 in the past. Group and reason codes come from the standard X12 code list, so remits can be routed automatically to the right work queue ([X12](https://x12.org/codes/claim-adjustment-reason-codes)). A person still has to fix the underlying cause and resubmit or appeal. Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

## Related guides

- [Denial management (hub)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/)
- [CO-22: coordination of benefits](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-22/)
- [CO-197: authorization absent](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-197/)
- [What is revenue cycle management?](https://medicalbillingteam.com/what-is-revenue-cycle-management/)
- [CO-97 bundling denials](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-codes/co-97/)

## FAQ

### What does denial code CO-204 mean?

X12 defines CARC 204 as "This service/equipment/drug is not covered under the patient's current benefit plan."

### How do I fix a CO-204 denial?

Confirm the exclusion with the payer, check coding, check whether a carve-out administrator should receive the claim, and ask about exceptions or appeals when clinically appropriate.

### Can I bill the patient for CO-204?

Check your contract, any advance-notice rules and state law first. A CO group code generally indicates the adjustment is the provider's responsibility.

### How is CO-204 different from CO-22?

CO-204 means the plan doesn't cover the service. CO-22 means another payer may be primary under coordination of benefits.

### How do I prevent CO-204 denials?

Verify benefits for the specific service before it's provided, identify carve-outs, and give advance notice of non-covered services where rules allow.

# Days in AR: how to calculate and reduce AR days

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** Days in AR (days in accounts receivable) is the average number of days it takes to collect payment, usually calculated as total A/R divided by average daily charges. To reduce days in A/R, measure it the same way every month, submit clean claims quickly, and work unpaid claims by dollar value and age. Fix the eligibility and authorization errors at the front end, post payments daily, and handle patient balances in their own workflow. Most of these steps depend on having enough dedicated follow-up time.

Days in accounts receivable (A/R) is the number most practice owners look at first, because it answers a simple question: how long does it take us to get paid? This guide explains how to measure it, the workflow that brings it down, and how to staff A/R follow-up so it actually happens. It's part of our [revenue cycle management staffing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/) series.

We won't promise a target number of days. Results depend on your specialty, payer mix and starting point. What we can describe is the process that consistently moves the number in the right direction.

## Step 1: Measure days in A/R the same way every month

A common formula:

1. Add your gross charges for the last 90 days (or 3 months).
2. Divide by 90 to get **average daily charges**.
3. Divide **current total A/R** by average daily charges.

Example: $900,000 in charges over 90 days = $10,000 per day. Total A/R of $400,000 ÷ $10,000 = 40 days in A/R. (Illustrative arithmetic only, not a benchmark.)

Track alongside it:

- **A/R by aging bucket:** 0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 91-120, 120+ days.
- **Percentage of A/R over 90 days** (or over 120).
- **A/R by payer**, so you can see which payers are slow.
- **Insurance vs patient A/R**, which need different workflows.

Credit balances, unposted payments and stale charges distort the number, so clean those up first. See our [RCM KPI definitions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/).

## Step 2: Get claims out fast and clean

You can't collect what you haven't billed.

- **Charge lag:** measure days from date of service to charge entry; aim to enter charges daily.
- **Claim scrubbing:** run edits before submission.
- **Rejections:** work clearinghouse and payer rejections every day. A rejected claim sitting for two weeks adds two weeks to A/R and inches toward timely filing limits. Medicare generally requires claims within one calendar year of the date of service ([CMS Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 1, §70](https://www.cms.gov/regulations-and-guidance/guidance/manuals/downloads/clm104c01.pdf)); many commercial payers allow less time.

## Step 3: Work A/R by priority, not by alphabet

A/R follow-up fails when staff start at the top of an alphabetical list every Monday. Instead:

1. **Sort by dollar value and age.** Work high-dollar claims in the 31-60 and 61-90 buckets first. They're old enough to need attention and young enough to fix.
2. **Group by payer.** One call or portal session can resolve several claims.
3. **Check status before calling.** Use payer portals and 276/277 claim status transactions where available.
4. **Act on what you find:** resubmit, send records, correct coding, bill secondary, or route to [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/).
5. **Set a follow-up date** for every claim touched and document the action.
6. **Escalate** claims stuck with a payer past its own processing commitments.

## Step 4: Fix the front-end causes

Much aging A/R starts at check-in. In a 2025 vendor survey, billers named coordination of benefits (45%), non-coverage (39%) and prior authorization or referral issues (31%) as top denial reasons, along with inaccurate demographics (25%) ([Tebra](https://www.tebra.com/theintake/getting-paid/medical-billing-pain-points-insights-solutions)). Each of these turns into aging A/R.

- Verify eligibility and benefits before every visit.
- Confirm authorizations and track visit limits and expiration dates.
- Capture insurance cards and demographics accurately at every visit.
- Collect copays and known patient balances at the time of service.

Our [eligibility verification and prior authorization guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/) covers this in detail.

## Step 5: Post payments accurately and promptly

Payment posting is where you discover underpayments, partial denials and secondary claims that need to go out. Post ERAs daily, reconcile to bank deposits, and flag:

- payments below contracted rates;
- zero-pay lines (these are denials);
- claims needing secondary or tertiary billing; and
- patient responsibility that should move to patient statements.

## Step 6: Handle patient A/R separately

Patient balances need statements, reminders, payment plans and clear communication, not payer calls. Keep the two workflows separate so neither gets neglected.

## Step 7: Clean up old A/R deliberately

For claims over 120 days:

- Check whether they can still be corrected or appealed within payer limits.
- Work the highest-value recoverable claims first.
- Write off only under your written policy, with documentation and approval.

Old A/R cleanup is often a short project that benefits from temporary extra hands.

## Staffing A/R follow-up

The most common reason A/R grows is simple: nobody has protected time to work it. Front-desk staff and office managers get pulled into phones and patients. Signs you need dedicated A/R capacity:

- A/R over 90 days is rising month over month.
- Claims are aging past timely filing or appeal limits.
- Follow-up happens in bursts, then stops.
- One person holds all the payer knowledge.

Options:

- **Add an in-house A/R specialist.** Good control; recruiting and turnover risk.
- **Outsource to a billing company.** Hands-off; less visibility.
- **Add a dedicated remote A/R specialist** who works your queue in your systems, under your rules. This is the model our operator provides.

A good A/R specialist knows payer portals, reads remittances fluently, documents every touch and escalates sensibly. Payer phone calls during US business hours matter, so confirm schedule overlap. Before granting any access, put a business associate agreement and access controls in place ([HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/)).

## What to report monthly

- Days in A/R (same method every month)
- A/R over 90 and over 120 days, in dollars and percent
- A/R by payer
- Claims touched per specialist per day and follow-up dates met
- Denials received and resolved
- Write-offs by reason

This site is operated by [Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/), which provides remote billing staff including A/R follow-up and [data entry support](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/virtual-assistant-skills/data-entry/). If you'd like a second opinion on your A/R workload, request a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/) or use the [Medical Billing Health Checklist](https://medicalbillingteam.com/checklist/) to self-audit first.

## Common mistakes that keep A/R high

- **Working the oldest claims first, no matter what.** Very old, low-dollar claims may be past timely filing. Prioritize by dollar value and by what's still collectible.
- **Touching claims without a next step.** Every follow-up should end with a documented action and a date to check again.
- **Letting credits and unapplied payments sit.** They distort A/R reports and can create refund obligations.

**Approved vendor:** [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), which operates this site, provides dedicated remote staff for this work and signs a business associate agreement with each client before any PHI access. See [approved vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/) and [how we vet vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-we-vet-vendors/).

## Technology

Automated claim-status checks and A/R prioritization tools can show which claims need a call today, which helps lower days in A/R. AI assistants can summarize payer responses and draft follow-up notes for a person to review. Someone still has to make the calls and resolve the claims. Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

## Related guides

- [Denial management basics](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/)
- [Medical billing staffing cost comparison](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/)
- [Revenue cycle management staffing (main guide)](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)
- [What an AR specialist does](https://medicalbillingteam.com/ar-specialist/)
- [revenue cycle management basics](https://medicalbillingteam.com/what-is-revenue-cycle-management/)

## FAQ

### How do you calculate days in A/R?

A common method divides total accounts receivable by average daily charges. For example, add gross charges for the last 90 days, divide by 90 to get average daily charges, then divide current total A/R by that number. Use the same method every month so the trend is meaningful.

### What is a good number of days in A/R?

It varies by specialty, payer mix and calculation method, and many benchmark sources are member-only. Track your own trend and the share of A/R over 90 days, and compare with specialty data you trust.

### What is the fastest way to reduce A/R days?

Work high-dollar claims in the 31-90 day buckets before they age further, fix rejections daily, submit charges promptly, and stop recurring front-end errors such as eligibility and authorization problems.

### What does an AR follow-up specialist do?

They work unpaid and underpaid claims by age and value, check claim status in payer portals, call payers, correct and resubmit claims, route denials for appeal, and document every action.

### Should old A/R be written off?

Only under a written write-off policy after documented collection efforts, and with approval. Before writing off, check whether claims can still be corrected or appealed within the payer's limits.

# How we vet medical billing and RCM staffing vendors

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** Before we list a vendor, it has to sign a business associate agreement (BAA) with each client before any PHI access, give staff the minimum access they need, work in the client's systems under the client's workflows, show experience with US payers and billing tasks, provide references on request, and never claim to be "HIPAA certified." We also tell you plainly that this site is operated by Alliance Global Solutions, currently the only vendor on our list.

Most medical billing buyers' guides rank vendors without saying who pays for them. We'd rather show our criteria, apply them in public and be upfront about our interest. You can use the same list to evaluate any vendor, including ones we've never heard of.

## The criteria

A vendor must meet every one of these before we list it as an [approved vendor](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/).

### 1. Signs a BAA before any PHI access
A company that performs billing or other functions involving protected health information on a practice's behalf is a business associate under HIPAA and needs a written business associate agreement ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). We require that the BAA is signed before anyone logs in. See [business associate agreements and HIPAA](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/).

### 2. No "HIPAA certified" claims
HHS's Office for Civil Rights does not endorse, certify or recommend specific technology or products ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html)). A vendor that markets itself as "HIPAA certified" is overstating something, so we won't list it.

### 3. Dedicated people, working in your systems
We list staffing vendors whose people work your queues, in your practice management system, clearinghouse and payer portals, with access you grant and can revoke. You keep control of the process and your payer relationships. See [medical billing outsourcing: three models](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-outsourcing/).

### 4. Experience with US billing work
The vendor should be able to explain how its staff handle the work you need, such as [insurance verification](https://medicalbillingteam.com/eligibility-verification-prior-authorization/), [prior authorization](https://medicalbillingteam.com/prior-authorization-specialist/), claim follow-up, [denial management](https://medicalbillingteam.com/denial-management/), payment posting or [credentialing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/credentialing-services/), and how new staff are trained on your payers.

### 5. Hiring, supervision and continuity
Who recruits, screens and supervises the staff? What happens if someone is out or leaves? We ask vendors to explain their process in writing.

### 6. Minimum necessary access and secure remote work
HIPAA's minimum necessary standard means staff should see only what their role requires ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/minimum-necessary-requirement/index.html)). We ask how access is granted, logged and removed. These controls depend partly on your systems, so you should verify them during setup.

### 7. References on request
A vendor should be willing to connect you with references after an initial conversation. We don't publish client names or testimonials on this site.

### 8. Clear, honest pricing conversations
Pricing should be explained in writing before you sign, with no percentage-of-collections surprises if you're buying a staffing model. We don't publish vendor prices because they depend on roles and volume. See [medical billing staffing costs](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/).

## What we don't do

- We don't sell placements or rankings, and there is no paid tier.
- We don't publish star ratings, reviews or testimonials.
- We don't list vendors to make the page look bigger. Today the list has one vendor, [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), and it's the company that operates this site. You can read the company's own [about page](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/about-us/) to compare it with our criteria.
- We don't verify every safeguard on your behalf. Do your own due diligence and get your own legal and compliance advice.

## How listing works

A vendor that wants to be considered can [contact us](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/). We'd review it against the criteria above, ask for documentation and references, and disclose any financial relationship on its listing. We'll re-check listed vendors at least once a year and when we learn of a material change.

## Technology

Vendors increasingly pair staff with automation, from eligibility bots to AI assistants that draft appeals. Ask any vendor which tools touch PHI and whether each tool vendor signs a BAA, because a tool vendor handling PHI on your behalf is generally a business associate too ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. See [technology in medical billing](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/) for the latest updates.

**Affiliation disclosure:** Medical Billing Team is operated by Alliance Global Solutions. That means we have a financial interest in Alliance Global Solutions, currently the only vendor on our approved vendor list. Requests you submit through this site may be referred to Alliance Global Solutions, and we benefit if you hire it. We hold Alliance Global Solutions to the same [published criteria](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-we-vet-vendors/) we'd apply to any vendor, and we don't publish ratings, reviews or testimonials.

# How a remote medical billing team works

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** You tell us which billing work needs help. Alliance Global Solutions recruits dedicated remote staff for those roles, and they work in your systems, under your workflows, once a business associate agreement and access controls are in place. You direct the work; the staffing provider employs and supports the staff.

A dedicated remote billing team is people, not software. Here is what the process looks like from the first conversation to day-to-day work.

## Step 1: Tell us about your workload

Use the [short form on the home page](https://medicalbillingteam.com/#assessment) or the [longer contact form](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/). We ask for practice-level details only: specialty, number of providers, a collections range and your current setup. **Never include patient information.**

## Step 2: Free staffing assessment

A billing staffing specialist talks with you, usually for 20 to 30 minutes, about:

- which queues are falling behind (eligibility, authorizations, claims, denials, A/R, posting);
- your systems, payers and specialty-specific rules;
- whether your systems can support secure remote access;
- the hours and coverage you need; and
- whether a remote team is a sensible fit at all.

If it isn't, for example because your processes are undocumented or your payer contracts restrict offshore access, we'll tell you.

## Step 3: Meet candidates, sign agreements, onboard

If you decide to go ahead:

1. **Role definition.** We agree on tasks, hours, systems and how performance will be measured.
2. **Candidate interviews.** You interview shortlisted candidates and choose who joins your team.
3. **Agreements.** A services agreement and a **business associate agreement (BAA)** are signed before anyone receives access to protected health information. See our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/).
4. **Secure access setup.** Unique logins, multi-factor authentication, role-based permissions and secure remote access (VDI or VPN), with no local downloads.
5. **Training on your workflows.** Your procedures, payers, escalation rules and reporting.
6. **Ramp-up.** Start with a defined queue, review work closely in the first weeks, then expand.

## Day to day

- Staff work your queues during agreed hours, often overlapping US business hours.
- You set priorities and approve anything outside the agreed rules (write-offs, refunds, appeals strategy).
- You get regular reporting on volumes worked and the KPIs you choose, such as days in A/R or denial rate. See [RCM KPIs, defined](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/).
- You can add roles or reduce capacity under the terms of your agreement.

## What we don't do

- We don't ask for patient information through this website.
- We don't claim to be "HIPAA certified"; no such official certification exists.
- We don't promise specific outcomes before understanding your data.

**Approved vendor:** [Alliance Global Solutions](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/), which operates this site, provides dedicated remote staff for this work and signs a business associate agreement with each client before any PHI access. See [approved vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/) and [how we vet vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-we-vet-vendors/).

## Related guides

- [medical billing staffing FAQ](https://medicalbillingteam.com/faq/)
- [back to the Medical Billing Team home page](https://medicalbillingteam.com/)

## Technology

Once staff are onboarded, many teams add automation for eligibility checks and claim status, plus AI assistants that help draft appeals or summarize payer policies, with a person reviewing the output. Any tool that touches PHI should be approved by your practice and covered by a BAA where the tool vendor handles PHI ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

## FAQ

### Do remote staff use our software or theirs?

Yours. Dedicated staff work in your practice management system, clearinghouse and payer portals, with access you grant and can revoke at any time.

### Who manages the remote staff day to day?

You direct the work and set priorities. The staffing provider handles employment, HR, equipment, attendance and support, and can help with supervision and reporting.

### What do we need to have in place first?

A signed business associate agreement, a secure way for staff to reach your systems (ideally a virtual desktop or VPN with MFA), user accounts with role-based access, and documented procedures for the tasks you're assigning.

### Can we start with one person?

Yes. Many practices start with one role, such as eligibility verification or A/R follow-up, and add more once the workflow is running smoothly.

# Frequently asked questions

## About remote billing staff

### What is a remote medical billing team?

Dedicated billing and revenue cycle staff who work remotely in your systems, under your workflows. You direct the work; a staffing provider recruits, employs and supports the staff. [How it works →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-it-works/)

### How is a staffing model different from outsourcing to a billing company?

A billing company usually takes over the billing function, often for a percentage of collections. With a staffing model you get dedicated people working your queues in your software, and you keep control of the process and payer relationships. [Cost comparison →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/)

### What roles can remote staff cover?

Common roles include billing and claims specialists, A/R follow-up, denial follow-up, eligibility and benefits verification (VOB), prior authorization, payment posting, coding (with credentials), credentialing and admissions or intake support. [RCM staffing guide →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/)

### Do you work with medical billing companies?

Yes. Billing companies often add dedicated remote staff as they take on new clients. Our approved vendor's clients include large billing companies that handle billing for multiple clients.

## HIPAA and security

### Is anyone 'HIPAA certified'?

No. There is no official HIPAA certification for companies or individuals. HHS's Office for Civil Rights does not endorse or certify vendors. Ask about specific safeguards instead: a BAA, MFA, secure remote access, role-based access, training and incident response. Source: [HHS, cloud computing guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html). [HIPAA guide →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/)

### Will the staffing provider sign a business associate agreement?

A provider whose staff will access protected health information on your behalf is generally a business associate, and a BAA should be signed before any access. Have your counsel review it. Alliance Global Solutions signs a business associate agreement (BAA) with each client before any of its staff access protected health information. Source: [HHS, business associates](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html).

### Is offshore billing allowed under HIPAA?

HIPAA does not ban offshore work, but HHS notes that overseas arrangements can increase risk and raise enforceability questions. Address them in your risk analysis, and check payer and Medicaid contracts, some of which restrict offshore access.

## Cost and results

### How much does remote billing staff cost?

Pricing is usually per full-time staff member per month or per hour. Compare it with the fully loaded cost of a local hire and with billing company quotes using our cost worksheet. We don't publish generic price ranges. [Cost worksheet →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-staffing-cost/)

### Can you guarantee lower denials or fewer A/R days?

No. Results depend on your payers, specialty, documentation and processes. Anyone promising a specific reduction before reviewing your data should be asked how they can know that.

## Getting started

### What hours do remote staff work?

Schedules are agreed up front. Many teams overlap US business hours so they can call payers and handle same-day eligibility work.

### How long does it take to get started?

It depends on role definition, candidate interviews, agreements and access setup. The assessment call will give you a realistic timeline for your situation. [Request an assessment →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/)

### Can we start with one person?

Yes. Many practices start with one queue, such as eligibility or A/R follow-up, and expand once it runs smoothly.

## About this site

### Who operates this website?

This site is operated by Alliance Global Solutions, a provider of remote medical billing and revenue cycle staff. We may contact you about our services if you request it. [About & disclosure →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/)

### Should I include patient details in my inquiry?

No. Please do not include any patient information in forms, emails or chat. Practice-level details are all we need.

### How do I stop emails or calls?

Use the unsubscribe link in any email, reply STOP to texts, or tell us on a call. We honor opt-out requests promptly.

- [medical billing resource home](https://medicalbillingteam.com/)

## Technology

AI and automation now show up across billing, from claim scrubbing to electronic prior authorization, which CMS-0057-F requires impacted payers to support through APIs by January 1, 2027 ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/cms-interoperability-and-prior-authorization-final-rule-cms-0057-f)). Any tool vendor that handles PHI on your behalf is generally a business associate and needs a BAA ([HHS](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html)). Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)

# About this site

*By the Medical Billing Team editors · Published October 18, 2026 · Updated October 18, 2026 · [How we research and review](https://medicalbillingteam.com/about/#how-we-write-our-guides)*

**Short answer:** medicalbillingteam.com is an informational resource about medical billing and revenue cycle staffing, with a short list of [approved vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/) that meet our [published criteria](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-we-vet-vendors/). It is operated by Alliance Global Solutions, a provider of remote billing staff and currently the only approved vendor, so requests you send may be referred to it. Our guides cite public sources and make no outcome promises.

Medical Billing Team is a resource for US medical practices and billing companies that are sorting out how to staff their billing and revenue cycle work. We write plain-English guides on topics like denial management, A/R follow-up, eligibility and prior authorization, HIPAA safeguards for outsourced staff and the real costs of different staffing models.

## Disclosure: who operates this site

**This site is operated by Alliance Global Solutions, a provider of remote medical billing and revenue cycle staff. Alliance Global Solutions is currently the only vendor on our approved vendor list, and requests you submit here may be referred to it. We benefit financially if you hire it. We may contact you about our services if you request it.**

That means we have a commercial interest in the topics we write about. Alliance Global Solutions provides dedicated remote staff (US-based management and admin; staff in the Philippines, Colombia and other countries) for roles such as billing specialists, A/R follow-up, eligibility and insurance verification (VOB), prior authorization, payment posting, denial follow-up and admissions or intake support. You can learn more about the company on its own website: [about Alliance Global Solutions](https://www.allianceglobalsolutions.com/about-us/).

Alliance Global Solutions signs a business associate agreement (BAA) with each client before any of its staff access protected health information. We don't describe ourselves as "HIPAA certified," because there is no such certification.

We think you should know that before you read anything here, so this disclosure also appears in the footer of every page and next to our forms.

## How the approved vendor list works

This site works like a guide plus a short, vetted directory. We write the guides; when you ask for help, we route your request to an approved vendor.

- **Published criteria.** A vendor must meet every item on [how we vet vendors](https://medicalbillingteam.com/how-we-vet-vendors/), including signing a BAA with each client before any PHI access, dedicated staff working in the client's systems, US billing experience and references on request.
- **One vendor today, by design.** Our [approved vendor list](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/) has one company, Alliance Global Solutions, and it operates this site. We won't pad the list with vendors we can't stand behind, and we don't sell placements.
- **No ratings, reviews or testimonials.** We describe what a vendor does, in facts it has confirmed. See the [Alliance Global Solutions profile](https://medicalbillingteam.com/approved-vendors/alliance-global-solutions/).
- **Your contract is with the vendor.** If you hire a vendor, the agreement, including the BAA, is between your practice and that vendor. Do your own due diligence.

## How we write our guides

- **We explain options fairly**, including when in-house staff or a full-service billing company is a better fit than remote staff.
- **We cite public sources.** Any statistic on this site links to a public source such as CMS, HHS, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the AMA or KFF. Where we cite a vendor survey, we say so. If we can't find a reliable public source for a number, we leave the number out.
- **We don't promise results.** Billing outcomes depend on your payers, specialty, documentation and processes. We don't claim that any staffing model will cut denials or A/R days by a set amount.
- **No fake proof.** You won't find invented testimonials, star ratings, client logos or case studies here. If we ever publish a client story, it will be real, permission-based and clearly labeled.
- **We are not "HIPAA certified," and neither is anyone else.** There is no official HIPAA certification. We explain what safeguards to look for in our [HIPAA guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/).
- **Dates mean something.** Each guide shows its original publication date and the date of its last substantive update. We change the "Updated" date only when content meaningfully changes, not for a redesign or rebuild. Guides are reviewed at least quarterly and whenever CMS, HHS, payers or code sets change something they cover.
- **Who writes and reviews.** Guides are published under the Medical Billing Team editors byline. We don't invent author personas or credentials. When a named reviewer with medical billing experience checks a guide, their name and role will appear on it.
- **How we use automation.** We use AI tools to help research and draft. Every statistic and regulatory statement is checked against the linked public source before publishing, and the sources are linked inline.

# Medical Billing Health Checklist: a medical billing audit checklist

A one-page self-audit to find where your revenue cycle is leaking. Built for practice owners, office managers, billing managers and billing companies. It takes about 15 minutes and you don't need any patient data to complete it.

**Inside:**
- 43 yes/no checks across front end, claims, denials, A/R, payment posting, reporting, staffing and HIPAA
- A KPI worksheet with consistent definitions
- A simple staffing cost comparison worksheet

## Get the checklist (form)

Fields: Name · Work email · Practice or company name · Number of providers · Phone (optional)

> **Do not include any patient information.**

TCPA checkbox (optional, unchecked, shown only if phone entered): same text as the home page short form.

Email notice: "We'll email you the checklist and occasional guides about billing staffing. Unsubscribe any time."

Button: **Send me the checklist**

---

## How to use it

Answer each item **Yes**, **No** or **Not sure**. Every "No" or "Not sure" is a place to look first. This is a self-assessment, not an audit or legal review.

## 1. Front end: scheduling, eligibility and authorizations

- [ ] We verify eligibility and benefits before every visit, not just for new patients.
- [ ] We re-check insurance cards and demographics at every visit.
- [ ] We identify coordination of benefits (which plan is primary) before the visit.
- [ ] We maintain a current prior authorization matrix by payer and service.
- [ ] We track authorization expirations and visit limits.
- [ ] We give the front desk an estimated patient responsibility to collect at check-in.
- [ ] We identify behavioral health carve-outs during eligibility checks (if applicable).

## 2. Charges and claims

- [ ] Charges are entered within 1-2 business days of the date of service.
- [ ] Claims are scrubbed before submission.
- [ ] Clearinghouse and payer rejections are worked daily.
- [ ] We track timely filing limits for each major payer.
- [ ] Coding is done or reviewed by credentialed coders for our specialty.
- [ ] We updated our systems for this year's code changes (ICD-10-CM changes Oct 1; CPT/HCPCS changes Jan 1, plus quarterly updates).

## 3. Denials

- [ ] Every denial lands in one queue with a named owner.
- [ ] Denials are categorized by payer and reason.
- [ ] Denials are worked at least weekly, by deadline and dollar value.
- [ ] Appeals are tracked with deadlines and outcomes.
- [ ] Top preventable denial reasons are reviewed monthly and fed back to the front desk and coders.

## 4. Accounts receivable

- [ ] We calculate days in A/R the same way every month.
- [ ] We review A/R by aging bucket and by payer monthly.
- [ ] A/R follow-up is prioritized by dollar value and age, not alphabetically.
- [ ] Every touched claim has a documented action and next follow-up date.
- [ ] We have a written write-off policy with approval levels.
- [ ] Patient A/R has its own workflow (statements, reminders, payment plans).

## 5. Payment posting

- [ ] ERAs are posted daily and reconciled to bank deposits.
- [ ] Zero-pay and partial-pay lines are flagged as denials.
- [ ] We compare payments to contracted rates to catch underpayments.
- [ ] Secondary claims go out promptly after primary payment.
- [ ] Credit balances are reviewed and resolved regularly.

## 6. Reporting

- [ ] Leadership sees a monthly KPI report (see worksheet below).
- [ ] We can see each staff member's queue and output.
- [ ] We know our top 5 payers by A/R and by denials.

## 7. Staffing and coverage

- [ ] More than one person can do each critical billing task.
- [ ] Billing staff have protected time (they aren't constantly pulled to the front desk).
- [ ] Procedures for each queue are documented.
- [ ] We have a plan for vacations, leave and turnover.
- [ ] We've compared our fully loaded in-house cost with other options (see worksheet).

## 8. HIPAA safeguards for vendors and remote staff

- [ ] Every vendor or agency with PHI access has a signed BAA.
- [ ] Every user has a unique login with multi-factor authentication.
- [ ] Remote access uses a VPN or virtual desktop; local downloads are blocked.
- [ ] Access is role-based and removed the same day someone leaves.
- [ ] Our HIPAA risk analysis includes remote and offshore access.
- [ ] Vendors must notify us of incidents within a defined timeframe.

See the [HIPAA guide for outsourced billing staff](https://medicalbillingteam.com/hipaa-outsourced-medical-billing/) for the full question list.

## KPI worksheet

| KPI | Definition | This month | Last month | 3 months ago |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Days in A/R | Total A/R ÷ (charges for last 90 days ÷ 90) | | | |
| A/R over 90 days (%) | A/R aged 91+ days ÷ total A/R | | | |
| Denial rate | Denied claims ÷ claims submitted | | | |
| Clean claim rate | Claims accepted on first submission ÷ claims submitted | | | |
| Net collection rate | Payments ÷ (charges − contractual adjustments) | | | |
| First-pass resolution | Claims paid/resolved on first submission ÷ claims submitted | | | |
| Charge lag (days) | Average days from date of service to charge entry | | | |

Benchmarks vary by specialty and source; track your trend. Definitions are explained in our [RCM staffing guide](https://medicalbillingteam.com/revenue-cycle-management-staffing/).

## Staffing cost worksheet

| Line | In-house (per FTE) | Billing company | Remote staff (per FTE) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base cost | Wage × hours | Fee × monthly collections | Quoted rate |
| Benefits & taxes | (BLS: benefits ≈ 30% of private-industry compensation costs, June 2026) | Included | Included in rate (confirm) |
| Recruiting/training | | | |
| Software seats | | | |
| Equipment/remote access | | | |
| Management time | | | |
| **Monthly total** | | | |

Source for the benefits share: [BLS Employer Costs for Employee Compensation](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ecec.nr0.htm).

## Scoring

- **0-5 "No/Not sure":** solid foundation; focus on fine-tuning.
- **6-15:** specific gaps; pick the section with the most "No" answers and fix it first.
- **16+:** the revenue cycle likely needs more structure or capacity. Consider a [free staffing assessment](https://medicalbillingteam.com/contact/).

(Scoring bands are a simple rule of thumb, not a validated benchmark.)

## Technology

When you run this audit, check which steps are already automated (eligibility checks, claim scrubbing, claim status) and which still depend on manual work. Large RCM vendors are moving payer-policy checks to the front end so requirements are visible before care is delivered ([Fierce Healthcare](https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/health-tech/thoreau-backed-ensemble-penelope-health-partner-tackle-payer-denials-upstream)). Alliance Global Solutions helps clients set up AI assistant workflows alongside their dedicated staff. [Latest updates in medical billing technology →](https://medicalbillingteam.com/medical-billing-technology/)
